nodes.description:
Azure is Microsoft's cloud computing platform offering a wide range of services—including compute, networking, data platform, storage, monitoring, serverless, cloud-native applications, databases, caching, and PaaS/SaaS capabilities—for deploying and managing applications and workloads, including AI workloads, AI services, SAP workloads, and HPC (High-Performance Computing) workloads. Specific services include Azure Functions, Azure Logic Apps, Azure Event Grid, Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Cognitive Search, Azure Blob Storage, Azure Container Apps, Azure Policy, Azure Files, Azure NetApp Files, Azure Load Testing, Azure Advisor, ExpressRoute, Virtual WAN, VPN Gateway, Virtual Network, confidential virtual machines, container services, Azure Monitor, Application Insights, Log Analytics, autoscale, Azure Virtual Desktop, Azure VMware Solution, and integrated AI features, among others. Azure provides hosting environments, VMs, networking, infrastructure services, automation, and monitoring solutions tailored for SAP and HPC workloads specifically.

Azure provides constructs such as management groups, subscriptions, and resource groups that promote segmentation, resource organization, capacity allocation, rate limiting, and priority queue processing. The platform supports infrastructure for vertical and horizontal scaling, load balancing, load testing, partitioning strategies, and architecture best practices to accommodate diverse workload requirements. Its geographically spread datacenters, regions, and Availability Zones around the world—powered by different energy sources—support zone-redundant and multi-region deployment approaches for mission-critical and highly available solutions, including multi-region data replication. Regions and infrastructure are key considerations in disaster recovery planning, with built-in failover and backup capabilities through PaaS solutions and managed services. Azure handles operational overhead for managed services like AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service).

Azure offers infrastructure services, SLAs, various SKUs, licensing models, and encryption models. Its SLAs should be considered in SLO calculations. The platform provides base-level encryption services, uses TLS 1.2 by default for data transmission, and supports both Microsoft-managed and customer-managed encryption keys. Identity and access management is provided by Microsoft Entra ID. The platform includes native security controls, RBAC, virtual networking, service tags, firewalls, security groups, and managed services for authentication, encryption, scaling, and ingress protection. Microsoft publishes security recommendations and supports denial of service attack simulations and timely notifications on service health and security breaches. Azure also provides tools for building compliant solutions and securing SAP workloads.

As a hyperscale cloud environment, Azure supports differing feature-sets across languages, SDKs, and APIs, with built-in retry mechanisms tuned to specific services. Azure natively supports Infrastructure as Code tools like Bicep and Terraform, and provides native automation tools including autoscaling and failover capabilities. Azure enables MLOps workflow solutions and serves as the target platform for the Microsoft Well-Architected Framework. The platform offers elasticity, scalability, and automation features well-suited for delivering SaaS workloads, managed applications, VMware workloads, Azure Virtual Desktop workloads, and sustainable workloads. Azure provides services for building sustainable applications, tracking carbon emissions, and designing workloads with consideration for cost and carbon efficiency.

Azure provides comprehensive cost management and optimization capabilities, including pricing calculators, billing tools, cost alerts, budgets, cost forecasts, tag inheritance, optimization discounts such as reservations, built-in policies, and advisory tools. The platform offers migration services and learning resources to support users in building cloud expertise. Organizations use Azure to deploy and test workloads across diverse scenarios.

Additionally, Azure refers to a network policy plugin for AKS that uses Linux IPTables to enforce specified network policies.

nodes.description:
The Azure Well-Architected Framework is a set of guiding tenets and design pillars developed by Microsoft for improving the quality of workloads on the Azure platform. Its five core pillars are Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, and Performance Efficiency. The framework is structured in a layered approach encompassing pillars, workload guidance, service guides, and design guides, providing fundamental guidance including design principles, recommendation guides, checklists, tradeoff analysis, and maturity models. It addresses nonfunctional requirements such as operability, cost, security, and efficiency, serving as a foundation for architectural excellence in cloud workload design.

Under Reliability, the framework features checklist recommendations such as RE:09 for disaster recovery planning. Under Security, it provides recommendations including SE:01 for establishing security baselines. Under Operational Excellence, it offers guidance covering incident management, Infrastructure as Code (IaC) best practices, and safe deployment practices. It also includes detailed Performance Efficiency guidelines and a dedicated Cost Optimization checklist for optimizing cloud workload costs. Beyond these five pillars, the framework is extended by sustainability design principles, with the Cost Optimization pillar containing guidance relevant to sustainability and a dedicated series on sustainable workloads.

The framework covers workload monitoring, optimizing workload design using flows, evaluating return on investment, trade-off analysis, and review assessments. It offers a mission-critical workload series focused on designing mission-critical applications on Azure. It serves as the benchmark against which the SaaS workload assessment checks alignment, and its pillars inform application delivery guidelines and cloud workload readiness assessments.

The Azure Well-Architected Framework also provides specific guidance for multiple workload types, including Azure Virtual Desktop workloads (with networking guidelines, storage design considerations, and best practices), Azure VMware Solution customizations and cloud readiness, SAP workloads, and HPC (high-performance computing) workload design recommendations. Overall, it serves as comprehensive architectural documentation providing actionable principles, checklists, and best practices for building reliable, secure, cost-effective, efficient, and sustainable cloud workload architectures on the Azure platform.<SEP>The Azure Well-Architected Framework (WAF) provides design principles and pillars that guide architectural decisions for HPC workloads.

Deployment Stamp is an architecture pattern used as a regional deployment unit for provisioning, scaling, and managing mission-critical workloads. It covers related infrastructure and application components together, functioning as a scale unit within a region. The pattern enables scaling complex workloads by treating the entire solution as a single unit rather than scaling individual components independently.

Each deployment stamp is typically placed in a dedicated subscription, ensuring that subscription limits apply only within a single stamp. A stamp can be constrained to a single availability zone, with multiple stamps deployed across zones to provide redundancy. In some implementations, deployment stamps are treated as ephemeral, short-lived units whose lifecycle is tied to a single release, with both infrastructure and application deployed together.

Azure Landing Zone is a foundational deployment framework and conceptual architecture in Microsoft Azure that depicts the overall cloud footprint for an organization with multiple subscriptions. It provides a subscription-based environment dedicated to applications, establishing clear management boundaries and supporting integration with broader organizational network topology.

Azure Landing Zone offers connectivity to on-premises data centers and networks through technologies such as ExpressRoute or virtual networks. It includes deployment configurations such as Online and Corp. Connected variants, catering to different network connectivity scenarios. The framework incorporates security capabilities including Azure Firewall or equivalent network virtual appliance (NVA) resources, providing centralized threat mitigation.

The framework includes common design areas, reference architecture, reference implementation, and processes to tailor deployments to specific design requirements. Centralized baseline policy assignments are applied at both management group and subscription levels, and centralized storage of operational data enables data forking to both centralized tooling and application-dedicated Log Analytics workspaces.

The Azure Landing Zone model describes a partnership where workload teams rely on platform teams for shared infrastructure and services, reflecting its role as a collaborative organizational deployment pattern.

nodes.description:
Autoscaling is a best practice method for automatically adjusting computing resources in response to changing demand and load levels. It works by adding or removing resources when predefined conditions, rules, or thresholds are met, encompassing both vertical scaling (up/down) and horizontal scaling (out/in). These thresholds are configured based on service-internal and application-set parameters, involving policies, cooldown periods, and configurable maximum and minimum limits.

Autoscaling balances workload supply against demand by dynamically allocating and deallocating resources, optimizing both resource allocation and cost efficiency for flows with variable demand. It is generally preferred over manual scaling for handling unexpected load and serves to protect workloads against unanticipated bursts in activity.

Autoscaling is widely available across Azure services and platforms. In PaaS offerings, it is commonly a built-in feature. In Application Gateway v2, it scales based on application traffic requirements. In Azure Container Apps, it dynamically manages loads based on HTTP requests, TCP connections, or custom metrics, including the ability to scale to zero. For Azure Functions, it automatically adjusts capacity based on demand. In Azure Databricks, it operates as a policy-driven mechanism that adds or removes nodes based on workload demands. For compute clusters, it can scale resources down to zero nodes when idle. It is also used in model deployment environments, adjusting the number of instances of a deployed model to match demand.

Despite its benefits, autoscaling has limitations. It may not handle sudden bursts well due to provisioning time required for new resources. It can also be misconfigured, potentially leading to excess cost or uncontrolled growth. Designing precise scale-out and scale-in strategies with appropriate limits is essential to its effective operation.<SEP>Autoscaling adds or reduces cluster nodes on demand for secondary node types to optimize resource usage.<SEP>Autoscaling automatically adjusts application resources based on demand factors like CPU utilization and incoming requests.<SEP>Autoscaling automatically increases and decreases resources based on application load to optimize performance and cost.

Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a managed Kubernetes platform on Azure that provides container orchestration capabilities for deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications and workloads. It supports cluster and node upgrades, networking, monitoring, governance, security, and cost optimization, with extensive policy and architecture support and best practices for cluster and workload management.

AKS has a hard requirement for an underlying virtual network and requires network integration configuration. It supports both Azure CNI and Kubenet networking plugins and can be optimized with accelerated networking for query-intensive workloads. The service has a scale limit of 1,000 nodes per cluster and supports automatic scaling for consumer workloads. It is monitored for CPU utilization and deployment statuses.

AKS serves as a primary application platform and compute environment, using container images from container registries and allowing health endpoint configuration for pods. It supports deploying containerized applications to improve parallel processing. Clusters can be bootstrapped using GitOps and Flux v2 for configuration management. PaaS (Platform as a Service) is a category of cloud computing services that provides a platform for developing, running, and managing applications without the complexity of maintaining underlying infrastructure. It is a cloud hosting model that simplifies provisioning and management of resources under a unified cost, often proving more economical than IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) due to lower operational costs.

PaaS solutions provide ready-made replication, failover, and backup capabilities, offloading maintenance responsibilities to the cloud provider. The model includes local redundancy by default and eliminates the need to collect operating system performance data, as the platform abstracts away operating system-level concerns.

In the context of Azure cloud services, PaaS resources can be isolated using network security perimeters. However, PaaS may have limitations regarding legacy or proprietary software, as its managed environment may not support all traditional or custom application frameworks.<SEP>Platform-as-a-service solutions can significantly reduce operational overhead and lower costs compared to virtual machine deployments.<SEP>Platform as a service (PaaS) is a hosting model that allows deploying applications without managing underlying infrastructure, with built-in autoscaling and load balancing.<SEP>Platform as a Service (PaaS) refers to managed cloud services that are highly optimized and operate more efficiently than traditional infrastructure.

Throttling is a design pattern that imposes limits on the rate or throughput of incoming requests to a resource or component. Its primary purposes include preventing resource exhaustion, supporting graceful degradation under heavy load, and mitigating congestion. Throttling controls resource consumption by deferring lower-priority operations when load thresholds are reached, helping avoid noisy neighbor scenarios and protecting against automated abuse.

By providing clear upper bounds on utilization, the Throttling pattern also informs resource sizing and cost modeling, enabling organizations to plan capacity more effectively.<SEP>Practice of limiting the rate of requests to a service or resource to protect it from overload.

Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, fully managed NoSQL and document database service on the Microsoft Azure platform. As a PaaS offering, it abstracts infrastructure complexity and automatically distributes workloads across instances, zones, and regions. It supports multiple database types including NoSQL, relational, vector, and table databases, with flexible schema supporting both transactional and analytical workloads. It is commonly used as a managed nonrelational data store for SaaS solutions, agent state persistence, and batch inference scenarios requiring fast, globally distributed access.

Azure Cosmos DB provides multi-region read and write capabilities with transparent replication, conflict resolution options, and service-managed failover. It does not require automated failover configuration when multi-write deployment is enabled, offers higher SLAs for multiregion deployments, and is particularly recommended for applications spanning more than four regions. It includes Availability Zone redundancy and native, non-configurable global retry capabilities.

The service offers tunable consistency levels, multiple API support, and configurable authentication methods including role-based access control (RBAC), private endpoints, and virtual network endpoints. Key data management features include automatic partition rebalancing, partitioning and sharding capabilities, customizable indexing policies (including composite indexes, index aliasing, and a default policy), support for concurrency, transactional batch operations, bulk operations, and built-in Time to Live (TTL) for managing data growth and document lifecycle management.

Azure Cosmos DB natively supports vector data types and vector search capabilities. It provides a change feed capability and an analytical column store that enables large-scale analytics without impacting transactional performance. It integrates with Azure Synapse for big data analytics and is commonly used to store "hot" data actively used by applications, such as product catalogs and e-commerce orders.

Automatic backups are taken at regular intervals without affecting performance, with multiple backup modes including periodic and continuous backup with point-in-time restore. Throughput can be scaled using request units (RUs) with provisioned throughput, autoscale throughput, and serverless models, returning a 429 status code when capacity is exceeded. Server-side latency is tracked as a key monitoring metric with dedicated monitoring insights. The service is commonly used as a downstream dependency within regional deployment stamps and is referenced in mission-critical data platform guidance.

Availability Zones are physically separate datacenter locations within an Azure region, each equipped with independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure. They follow a 3+1 datacenter model and are designed to provide datacenter-level fault tolerance, high availability, and fault isolation, with less than 2 milliseconds latency between them.

Availability Zones maximize resilience by distributing workloads across these physically separated datacenters within a region. This includes VMs, AKS agent nodes, data replicas, Azure Firewall instances, Application Gateway instances, log data replicas, and message data and metadata. Zone redundancy ensures resiliency to zone failures through automatic failover, routing traffic to other zones if one fails. Services including Azure Cosmos DB, Service Fabric clusters, and other regional deployments benefit from this distribution. When used with Azure Standard Load Balancer, Availability Zones enable a 99.99% SLA, and deploying Azure Firewall across multiple zones similarly provides higher SLA and resiliency.

Availability Zones are recommended for critical workloads to improve reliability and are considered fundamental infrastructure isolation units within Azure regions. They enable organizations to distribute solution components—including session hosts—for maximum availability, redundancy, and resilience, while reducing the risk of localized datacenter outages without significantly increasing cost or complexity. However, Availability Zones are limited to specific regions, and spreading resources across zones can affect performance due to inter-zone latency, which may be particularly disruptive for low-latency on-premises applications.<SEP>Availability zones are distinct locations within an Azure region used for redundancy.<SEP>Availability zones are separate datacenter locations used to distribute applications for fault tolerance.<SEP>Availability Zones provide an opportunity to create highly available ASCS architecture.<SEP>Availability Zones are the recommended option for deploying SAP application servers for resiliency on Azure.

Distributed Tracing is a diagnostic and observability technique used to track, monitor, and correlate requests as they flow through distributed systems and across service boundaries. It works by assigning unique activity IDs or correlation IDs to requests, enabling the linking of related events across multiple components and services. By capturing and correlating telemetry from metrics, logs, and traces across different application components or tiers, it builds end-to-end transaction flows that provide comprehensive insights into system behavior.

Distributed Tracing enables easier analysis of application performance data, helping identify performance bottlenecks, latency issues, and errors through root cause analysis. It can be applied at the transaction level to analyze bottlenecks across event delivery pipelines and other critical system flows. It also serves as a standard for propagating correlation across services to enable end-to-end traceability.

Tools such as Application Insights facilitate Distributed Tracing by providing comprehensive error messages with correlation IDs for end-to-end tracing across services, offering a unified view of system behavior. The complexity of distributed tracing increases when additional reliability components are introduced into an architecture, as more services and layers add to the volume of trace data that must be captured and correlated. Despite this complexity, it remains essential for maintaining observability in modern distributed systems.

Application Insights is an Application Performance Monitoring (APM) tool and a feature/extension of Azure Monitor. It is an extensible service for monitoring live applications, collecting application telemetry data including logs, metrics, traces, request rates, response times, exception details, and usage and performance data. It provides deep insights into application performance, availability, reliability, and application-related issues throughout development, testing, and production.

Application Insights automatically detects performance anomalies through its smart detection feature, which can analyze memory consumption and identify memory leaks. It helps identify and optimize hot paths in code by analyzing execution times and resource usage, and can monitor application usage to identify underutilized features. It provides configurable sampling percentages to balance visibility and performance.

Application Insights provides end-to-end tracing, dependency mapping, and user behavior analytics. It supports OpenTelemetry-based distributed tracing data collection and provides correlation IDs for error tracking, enabling users to query, correlate, and visualize application traces. Its SDK collects telemetry from producer and consumer applications, enabling end-to-end transaction tracing across them, including tracing from publishers through Service Bus to consumers. It supports custom metrics tracking for consumer-specific processing times and end-to-end latency. It also provides basic availability tests and Real User Monitoring (RUM) data capture for websites, and hosts the User Flow tool for analyzing user behavior.

Key features include application map, failure and performance views, profiling, smart detection, sampling capabilities, telemetry ingestion, instrumentation, alerting, and dashboards. Application Insights is integrated with API Management as an observability tool and is used for centralized monitoring of function performance, key metrics, and detailed insights into function operations. It can also be enabled to monitor online endpoints and deployments in machine learning scenarios.

Application Insights can be deployed in a workspace-based model underpinned by Log Analytics, requiring a Log Analytics workspace to function, and is billed through that workspace. As an Azure Monitor resource, it must be deployed and configured to incorporate data collection and querying capabilities.<SEP>Application Insights is a monitoring service used alongside Azure Monitor for workload observability.<SEP>Application Insights provides a detailed view of the time that workload requests spend in the network.<SEP>Application Insights is a tool for monitoring performance in Azure Virtual Desktop environments.<SEP>Application Insights is a tool used for performance monitoring in Azure Virtual Desktop.<SEP>Application Insights is a monitoring tool that can be used to build application dashboards.<SEP>Application Insights is a tool for tracking dependencies such as databases, API calls, and external services.

Azure ExpressRoute is a network connectivity service that provides private connectivity between on-premises networks and Microsoft Azure through dedicated circuits. It serves as a cloud connectivity solution and a typical external dependency for workloads, enabling clients outside Azure to access resources such as file shares through private networks as an alternative to public internet connections (e.g., opening TCP port 445).

Azure ExpressRoute includes components such as circuits, gateways, and Direct options. Microsoft provides guidance on resiliency and recoverability distinctions for the service, helping organizations design reliable hybrid connectivity architectures. It is commonly used to connect to on-premises services and access cloud workloads securely over private network paths.<SEP>Azure ExpressRoute is a service for enterprise network flows providing dedicated connectivity.<SEP>Azure ExpressRoute extends on-premises networks into Azure cloud over a private connection.<SEP>Azure ExpressRoute provides private network connectivity for Remote Desktop client users to connect to virtual networks.

A Health Model is a layered, iterative framework used to define, quantify, and aggregate the health of individual application components and the overall workload. It serves as a graphical representation of logical entities and their relationships, where each node has a health state definition that rationalizes monitoring data. The model represents application health using traffic light states—Healthy, Degraded, and Unavailable (or Unhealthy)—by defining these states for each component, critical flow, and workload to enable fast failure detection and recovery.

The Health Model correlates various monitoring data—including indicators, KPIs, and metrics reflecting business and operational objectives—to accurately reflect the runtime state of entities or an entire workload. It uses a distinct data schema optimized for observability, leveraging key resource-level metrics and scoring functions to quantify application health in the context of availability and performance requirements. This provides operators with in-depth visibility into system health, dependencies, and business impact as part of observability and reliability strategies.

The Health Model supports proactive monitoring by spotting early warning signs and triggering appropriate recovery processes based on defined disaster thresholds. It monitors component health through health endpoints, takes corrective action for non-transient failures, and alerts responsible parties. It can be integrated with alerts and CI/CD pipelines for calculating SLO attainment, enabling teams to detect and respond to issues and measure operational efficiency. The Health Model turns operational knowledge into actionable insights and is typically developed at Level 3 maturity to represent the overall health status of a workload, also supporting vendor support scenarios through its defined thresholds.<SEP>A health model is a graphical representation of logical entities and their relationships for a given scope, where each node has a health state definition to rationalize monitoring data.<SEP>A model that provides operators visibility into system health, dependencies, and business impact, using a distinct data schema optimized for observability.<SEP>A health model is a comprehensive framework that correlates various monitoring data to accurately reflect the runtime state of entities or an entire workload.<SEP>A health model is a framework for quantifying and visualizing the operational health states of workloads, applications, and infrastructure components.<SEP>A health model labels components as Healthy, Degraded, or Unhealthy according to service level objectives.<SEP>The Service Fabric health model is used to continuously monitor the health of a solution, including cluster health policies and application health policies.

nodes.description:
Azure App Service is a cloud platform service provided by Microsoft Azure for hosting web applications. It offers a comprehensive set of features designed to support the deployment, management, scaling, and security of web apps across various pricing and compute tiers.

App Service provides robust scaling capabilities, including autoscaling and per-app scaling, along with dedicated compute tiers and the Always On feature to ensure application availability. It supports zone redundancy for high availability, health checks, health probes, and automatic healing (auto-heal) to maintain application reliability.

For deployment and development workflows, App Service offers deployment slots that allow code to be deployed to nonproduction environments before production release. It also supports custom containers and the WebJobs feature for running background tasks.

From a security and networking perspective, App Service includes built-in authentication, managed identity support, TLS encryption, virtual network integration, and private endpoints to help secure applications and control network access.

App Service also provides diagnostic logging and diagnostics capabilities for monitoring and troubleshooting hosted applications, along with various pricing tiers to accommodate different workload requirements.<SEP>App Service is an Azure web-based resource that should be protected behind a WAF rather than exposed directly to the internet.

Azure Container Registry is a native Azure service for storing, managing, and hosting container images. It offers geo-replication capabilities, vulnerability scanning (including integration with Microsoft Defender), and supports Microsoft Entra ID authentication, enabling secure access from services like AKS. The registry supports automated container building and Docker builds for containerized development. It requires automated procedures for removing old image versions. By registering containers within Azure boundaries, it provides benefits in security, privacy, and proximity.
Auto Heal automatically recycles unhealthy workers to enable self-healing for mission-critical applications.

Health Check identifies non-responsive workers by assessing critical downstream dependencies.<SEP>Health check is a built-in App Service feature that periodically pings a web application path to determine application health and exclude unhealthy instances.

TCP port exhaustion occurs when outbound connections from a given App Service worker exceed capacity.<SEP>TCP port exhaustion occurs when outbound connections from a worker exceed capacity, depending on worker size.
Docker Hub is a public container registry that can lead to issues with service availability, throttling, and data exfiltration.

Log Analytics is an Azure service and tool within Azure Monitor used for ingesting, storing, querying, and analyzing operational data. It provides a robust built-in analytics capability for running queries against aggregated logs, enabling users to edit and run log queries within the Azure portal against data stored in Log Analytics workspaces.

Log Analytics workspaces serve as global unified data sinks for operational data from Azure resources such as Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Front Door, App Service, Azure Firewall, Event Grid, Event Hubs, Virtual WAN, SQL Managed Instance, and other resources. The service provides centralized log management and analysis, collecting and correlating usage, performance, and configuration data across Azure resources. It supports multi-tier log correlation with advanced trending capabilities, enabling visualization of log data from various sources. Workspaces receive streamed resource logs and support KQL (Kusto Query Language) queries for cross-instance analysis. They offer configurable daily caps, pricing tiers, retention policies, storage tiers, and ingestion-time transformation to reduce costs—particularly useful for selective firewall log processing—while also serving as the workspace-based service underlying Application Insights for log encryption and telemetry storage.

Log Analytics is used for auditing, logging, troubleshooting, alerting, compliance reporting, and security event analysis across multiple Azure services. It receives diagnostic logs from services like App Service, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Event Grid, Event Hubs, and Virtual WAN, and ingests MySqlAuditLogs through diagnostic settings for security event analysis. It supports querying diagnostic logs including TLS version violations and storing and analyzing Azure Firewall log data. It enables historical trend analysis through Kusto queries for Azure Database for MySQL performance monitoring, including slow query log analysis. Log Analytics integration supports advanced query and correlation of security events for SQL Managed Instance. It integrates with Microsoft Sentinel and Microsoft Defender for Cloud for security and monitoring purposes, and its exported data can be ingested into Azure Synapse for AIOps analysis and queried via Synapse Spark.

Log Analytics is also integrated with Azure Virtual Desktop, where it serves as a tool for performance monitoring, querying and analyzing diagnostics data, network information, and event logs for connections. It provides tables used as data sources for custom reporting and workbooks in Azure Virtual Desktop environments. The service has query limits and pricing tiers that may require optimization, particularly around concurrent query limits, with cost optimization guidance available for retention policies and storage tiers.<SEP>Log Analytics is an Azure service integrated with Azure VMware Solution for monitoring and analysis.<SEP>Log Analytics is an Azure service for collecting and querying logs, metrics, and diagnostic information.<SEP>Log Analytics collects guest-level logs and offers advanced integrations for alerting, visualization, querying, and machine learning-based insights.<SEP>Log Analytics is a service related to cost optimization in monitoring workloads.

Azure Event Hubs is a cloud-based, real-time event streaming platform and ingestion service offered as an Azure PaaS product. It can receive and process millions of events per second, supporting AMQP, Apache Kafka, and HTTPS protocols. The service is available in Standard, Premium, and Dedicated tiers.

Key features include partitioning, consumer groups, throughput units, retention policies, geo-disaster recovery, geo-replication, auto-inflate, custom dead-letter queues, security controls, and native programmatic retry capabilities scoped to the client. Best practices emphasize operational excellence, performance efficiency, and cost control.

Azure Event Hubs serves diverse roles across Azure architectures. It functions as a destination for diagnostic logs from services such as App Service, for routing audit logs, and for exporting Log Analytics workspace data (requiring the same region as the workspace). It can be triggered for automated actions and provides custom metrics for autoscaling in Container Apps. Azure API Management can connect to it using managed identities over private network connections.

In practical applications, Azure Event Hubs is used in scenarios such as e-commerce cart flows for real-time event processing and ingesting diagnostic logs to third-party tools, demonstrating its versatility as an asynchronous communication and event ingestion platform.<SEP>Azure Event Hubs is used by Azure Firewall to comprehensively log traffic metadata.<SEP>Azure Event Hubs supports external SIEM integration as an audit target.

Container registries host images deployed to container runtime environments like AKS, requiring careful configuration for mission-critical workloads.<SEP>Azure Container Registry is a service for hosting container images with support for geo-replication, zone redundancy, image locking, and private endpoints.<SEP>A dependent service for Machine Learning that should be configured with private endpoints and access regulated to approved registries only.

Microsoft Entra is a Microsoft identity provider (IdP) that provides centralized identity, authentication, access control, and authorization management across Azure services. It enables secure, credential-free authentication by allowing connections to services without using connection strings or keys.

Microsoft Entra supports identity-based authentication and role-based access control for numerous Azure services, including Azure Container Registry (integrated pushing and pulling of container images), Azure Cosmos DB (identity and role-based access control for authentication and resource management), Azure SQL Database, SQL managed instances, flexible servers, and Service Fabric clusters. For several of these services, Microsoft Entra supports Entra-only authentication, providing centralized identity management and enhanced security.

Microsoft Entra also provides custom roles used for authorization in a least privilege model, such as for Key Vault operations. Its activity logs can be exported to Log Analytics Workspace for monitoring and retention purposes.<SEP>Microsoft Entra provides group claims and identity information used for authorization and access control in knowledge tool calls.<SEP>Microsoft Entra tenant defines the boundary for identities that can manage Azure resources, used for identity management in SaaS solutions.<SEP>Microsoft Entra is a popular identity as a service (IDaaS) option used as both an enterprise and federated identity provider.<SEP>Microsoft Entra is Microsoft's identity service whose tenants are relevant for cross-tenant network connectivity scenarios.<SEP>Microsoft Entra provides tenant management capabilities used in organizing Azure resources.<SEP>Microsoft Entra is an identity and access management service that has trust relationships with Azure subscriptions.

Geo-replication is a feature of Azure Container Registry that replicates registries to multiple regions, providing resiliency against regional outages and reducing latency.<SEP>Geo-replication enables real-time asynchronous replication of events and metadata across multiple regions for Dedicated tier namespaces.<SEP>Geo-replication replicates events and metadata across multiple regions in real time for Dedicated tier namespaces.<SEP>Geo-replication replicates both metadata and message data across regions with synchronous and asynchronous modes, supporting planned and forced promotion scenarios.<SEP>Geo-replication replicates both metadata and message data across regions with automatic failover capabilities, offering synchronous and asynchronous replication modes.<SEP>Geo-replication provides automated regional failover with data replication for Service Bus namespaces.

Autoscale is a feature in Azure that automatically adjusts compute capacity and resources based on demand and predefined configurations. It ensures adequate resources are available by scaling out when any rule is met and scaling in when all rules are met, helping prevent overprovisioning and protecting against throttling errors.

Autoscale automatically adjusts throughput between a maximum value and 10% of that maximum based on application load. It can be configured through runbook automation to ensure elasticity in response to changing traffic patterns, such as for Azure Database for MySQL/PostgreSQL.

While Autoscale can scale down aggressively to reduce costs, this behavior may cause issues with sudden demand spikes or flapping, where resources oscillate between scaling up and down rapidly.<SEP>Autoscale automatically adjusts provisioned throughput to match actual workload needs.<SEP>Autoscale is a platform feature that helps optimize resource use by automatically adjusting capacity.
Per-app scaling allows an application to scale independently from the App Service plan that hosts it.

An App Service plan defines the compute resources for App Service, with a default soft limit of instances and support for multiple scale units and availability zone configuration.<SEP>An App Service plan determines the resources, operating system, region, and pricing model (SKU) used to host an app.<SEP>App Service plan determines resource limits, scaling capabilities, and compute units for hosted applications.<SEP>App Service plan defines the compute resources for hosting applications, with different tiers offering different compute options and pricing.

Azure Storage is a cloud storage service offered by Microsoft Azure that serves multiple purposes across data management, diagnostics, analytics, backup, and security scenarios.

Azure Storage functions as a destination for ingesting both application-level and platform-level diagnostic logs, including audit logs and Azure Firewall logged traffic metadata. It is used for "cold" operations data storage for analytical purposes and can serve as a target for custom backup implementations. Azure Storage accounts are used for backups, checkpoint locations, and cross-region replication. The service can be configured as a linked service and data source for Azure Synapse and serves as an export destination for Log Analytics workspace data. Azure Storage Accounts store operational data, exported Log Analytics data, and prepared machine learning training data. It can also host custom visuals and plugins for Grafana.

Azure Storage supports multiple redundancy options, including Zone-Redundant Storage (ZRS) and Geo-Redundant Storage (GRS), enabling zone-redundant deployments across multiple availability zones. In its GRS configuration, Azure Storage is recommended for long-term operational data storage exported from Log Analytics. The service offers multiple data access tiers, including an archive tier optimized for rarely accessed blob data with lowest storage costs but higher retrieval costs, along with lifecycle management policies.

Azure Storage automatically encrypts data at rest with block ciphers when persisted to a storage account. It provides account access key management including key rotation capabilities, along with blob storage, access control, and security configurations. The service offers native client retry support and TraceSource logging.

Azure Storage serves as a service dependency for Azure Event Hubs and should be tested for dependency failures in resilience scenarios. Azure Storage accounts are also permitted destinations for egress virtual network traffic in data exfiltration prevention configurations.<SEP>Azure Storage is a component accessed by the Analyst, Discriminative AI Data Scientist, and other personas.<SEP>Azure Storage is a storage service integrated with Azure Virtual Desktop.<SEP>Azure Storage is a storage platform used by Microsoft partner solutions for archive, backup, and disaster recovery workloads.
The active/passive deployment model is a multi-region strategy suitable for certain scenarios with lower reliability targets.

Geo-Redundant Storage (GRS) is an Azure Storage redundancy feature that automatically replicates data to a secondary paired region, ensuring data durability and protection against regional outages. It is the default storage option for periodic backups in Azure, with data replicated to a paired region.

GRS provides higher resilience than locally redundant storage, though at a greater cost, by synchronizing data across geographically separated regions. It is used in scenarios such as dead letter destinations in Azure Event Grid to protect undelivered events from regional failures. In Azure Files, GRS is supported only by standard SMB accounts.<SEP>GRS is an Azure Storage redundancy option that replicates data to other regions for protection against regional failures.<SEP>Geo-redundant storage (GRS) is an Azure Storage replication option for disaster recovery.<SEP>GRS replicates critical datasets and final results to survive regional failures.

nodes.description: Microsoft Entra Workload ID enables managed identities at the pod level in AKS.<SEP>Microsoft Entra Workload ID provides managed identities for AKS workloads.<SEP>Microsoft Entra Workload ID enables AKS workloads to access Microsoft Entra protected resources without managing credentials in code.<SEP>Microsoft Entra Workload ID is an open-source tool for protecting secrets and certificates in Key Vault.

Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management (IAM) platform that serves as the primary identity provider (IdP) for the Azure cloud platform. It provides authentication, authorization, and role-based access control (RBAC) capabilities across the Azure ecosystem, functioning as a shared foundational service and global platform dependency for almost all Azure services, covering the management plane and integrating with the data planes of most services.

As a global Azure service, Microsoft Entra ID is a managed service with built-in automatic redundancy across multiple regions, scaling transparently without user configuration. It offers centralized account management, application access management, enhanced identity protection, and managed identities that provide automatic identity management for applications—including VMs and scale sets—reducing human-operated tasks and reliability risks. The platform supports workload identity, service principals, and integration with numerous Azure services including Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Azure Container Registry, Azure Service Bus, App Service, Application Insights, Azure Database for MySQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, SQL Managed Instance, Container Apps, Azure Databricks, Azure Data Lake Storage, Event Grid, Event Hubs, Log Analytics workspaces, Azure NetApp Files, Service Fabric clusters, VPN gateways, and Azure Virtual Desktop. Native retry capabilities are embedded in the Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) for resilient authentication flows.

Microsoft Entra ID authenticates security principals and returns OAuth 2.0 tokens for authorization, providing token-based authentication as a secure alternative to basic authentication, shared keys, and shared access signatures. It provides enterprise authentication including single sign-on (SSO), credential passthrough for storage access, built-in Home Realm Discovery functionality, and integrates with App Service built-in authentication. The platform supports Conditional Access policies, serves as a standard identity provider for AI workloads, and supports document-level security integration.

Microsoft Entra ID provides identity-based access control with built-in mechanisms for key rotation and anomaly detection. Its advanced security features include multifactor authentication (MFA), passwordless authentication, Conditional Access policies, access reviews, permission management, threat intelligence, risk-based authentication, and access monitoring. The platform uses adaptive machine learning algorithms, heuristics, and known compromised credentials to detect suspicious actions, and provides Identity Protection capabilities and security groups for streamlined user management.

For Azure Virtual Desktop specifically, Microsoft Entra ID serves as the first-line authentication solution and is required for users to access the service. It provides identity and access management, Conditional Access, multifactor authentication, audit logs relevant to security compliance, and supports multi-forest scenarios with identity synchronization and management. For AKS clusters, it provides centralized identity management, authentication, RBAC, and cluster access control. Microsoft Entra ID is recognized as a critical external dependency for workloads in Failure Mode Analysis and is a recommended technology for security and access control across Azure environments.<SEP>Microsoft Entra ID is an identity service used for integrating workloads with robust IAM practices.<SEP>Microsoft Entra ID is an identity service integrated with Azure VMware Solution.<SEP>Microsoft Entra ID provides centralized user management with advanced security features including privileged identity management, multifactor authentication, and conditional access.<SEP>Microsoft Entra ID is a fully managed identity and access management service used to authenticate and authorize access to SAP systems and other applications.<SEP>Microsoft Entra ID provides authentication for HPC environments.

nodes.description: Kubernetes RBAC is used with Microsoft Entra ID for least privilege access control.<SEP>Kubernetes RBAC is used with Microsoft Entra ID for least privilege access control in AKS.<SEP>Kubernetes role-based access control is used with Microsoft Entra ID for least privilege access to cluster resources.<SEP>Kubernetes RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is a method for controlling access to the Kubernetes API server, integrated with Microsoft Entra ID.

Azure Policy is a governance and compliance service within the Azure Resource Manager control plane. It provides a comprehensive framework for enforcing and auditing security, reliability, and organizational standards across Azure platform services at scale. It supplements Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) by restricting actions that authorized users can perform, enforcing security and reliability configurations by remediating or prohibiting deviations at configuration time. An aggregated compliance dashboard and automatic remediation capabilities enable centralized visibility and enforcement.

Azure Policy drives compliance through enforced conventions, automated management activities, and compliance reporting, offering both custom options and built-in initiatives. It serves as an automated security governance tool that streamlines resource compliance with security baselines, protecting against configuration drift. It can enforce resource configurations such as enabling service firewalls, ensuring consistent diagnostic settings, controlling subnet traffic lacking network security groups, ensuring identity components like Key Vault use RBAC, disabling Azure Cosmos DB key-based metadata write access, and routing operational data to the correct Log Analytics workspace. It also enforces security controls like private endpoint usage, SSL enforcement, encryption, and resource locks across server instances while preventing costly database configurations. Additionally, Azure Policy provides drift detection and automatic remediation for gateway SKU compliance, diagnostic settings, and network security rules.

Azure Policy provides centralized governance safeguards for AKS clusters, including pod security, resource requests and limits, configuration baselines, and supports mission-critical workloads. Beyond security, it allows limiting resource types, SKUs, compute tiers, and instances through policy rules that enforce deployment restrictions, restrict deployment regions, enforce tagging policies, required tags, allowed tiers, and zone-redundancy requirements for production instances. It is also used to require approvals for high-cost changes, mandate reviews before adding capacity, and enforce mandatory tags on resource creation for cost allocation purposes.

Azure Policy provides extensive built-in policy definitions across numerous Azure services, including App Service, Application Insights, API Management, Application Gateway, Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, Container Apps, storage accounts, Azure Database for MySQL, Azure Databricks, Azure Disk Storage, Azure Files, Azure Firewall, Azure Front Door, Azure Functions, Event Grid, Event Hubs, ExpressRoute, Load Balancer, Log Analytics, Azure Machine Learning, Service Bus, Service Fabric, SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, Traffic Manager, Virtual WAN, Virtual Machines, Virtual Networks, and Azure Virtual Desktop. For SQL Database, built-in policies audit authentication, zone redundancy, backups, TLS, and auditing. For Azure Databricks, policies cover network security, encryption, and compliance auditing. For Event Hubs, it enforces throughput unit limits, restricts service tiers, and defines retention period policies. For Azure Machine Learning, policies audit network access, encryption, and authentication. For Service Bus, it enforces cost management by restricting tiers, regions, and expensive features. For Virtual Machines, it provides built-in definitions affecting compute layer security and dependencies. For Azure Virtual Desktop, it promotes consistency across VM configurations, insights, tagging, can ensure monitoring agents are installed on VMs, configure diagnostics settings, and audit session host operating systems for enterprise-scale compliance.

Azure Policy is used to implement policy-driven governance to help ensure security and compliance within enterprise technical estates. It applies security controls defined by the Microsoft cloud security benchmark and automates responses to Defender for Cloud recommendations. It works alongside Azure Arc to manage security configuration and compliance auditing for Azure Local, and is used for Azure Arc-enabled servers to audit and enforce security controls on guest VMs. It also manages the guest configuration feature used by Azure Automation State Configuration and ensures resource deployments adhere to organizational best practices. Policy artifacts should be regularly backed up with versioning.<SEP>Azure Policy is a tool for defining and enforcing policies to keep Azure virtual data centers continuously optimized for cost and sustainability.<SEP>Azure Policy is a service used to enforce VM governance for SAP workloads.<SEP>Azure Policy enforces security baselines and compliance reporting across HPC clusters to reduce misconfigurations and configuration drift.

Azure Monitor is a comprehensive, full-stack monitoring service provided by Microsoft Azure, enabled by default for all Azure subscriptions. It serves as a unified data platform for collecting, analyzing, and acting on operational data across cloud and on-premises environments, supporting three types of observability data: logs, metrics, and distributed traces. It automatically collects platform metrics, activity logs, diagnostics logs, and diagnostic data from various Azure resources, aggregating data from every layer and component of workloads across multiple Azure and non-Azure subscriptions and tenants. Pricing is based on data ingestion and retention, with Application Insights charges based on volume ingested and retention duration.

Azure Monitor is the overarching monitoring platform that includes Application Insights, alerts, workbooks, log queries, Log Analytics workspaces, and agents with data collection rules. It enables collection and analysis of telemetry data supporting capacity planning, demand forecasting, performance measurement, and cost optimization. It collects metrics, logs, and diagnostics from numerous services including AKS, Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Functions, Event Grid, Event Hubs, ExpressRoute, storage, API Management, Kubernetes clusters, Azure NetApp Files, VM instances, Azure Virtual Desktop, and Azure VMware Solution, providing near real-time operational insights. It is recommended for offloading observability concerns from workloads and provides a service map feature to automatically discover and visualize application and infrastructure components.

Azure Monitor integrates with Azure Databricks for viewing logs, collecting telemetry, enabling KQL queries, and supporting automated alerting, and provides custom dashboards and end-to-end transaction tracing through Application Insights integration. It also offers insight tools such as VM insights and network insights, workbooks for performance dashboards, integration with Azure Dashboards, resource logs for security investigations, diagnostic settings to capture security events, and data transformation features.

Azure Monitor provides an extensive alerting framework through Action Groups, covering metrics such as HA status, replication lag, CPU, memory, storage, throttling events, connection failures, and capacity shortages or scaling failures. For Azure Service Bus, it enables alerting on availability, throughput, authentication failures, throttling, and message volume patterns. It supports autoscale features, self-healing mechanisms, machine learning integration, and daily caps on workspaces, and is integrated with Azure Local for health, log, and metric alerts.

For SQL Managed Instance, Azure Monitor serves as a platform telemetry service for observability of health and workload performance, provides alerting for critical reliability metrics, offers real-time log analysis for audit events, and provides workbooks to surface operation trends. For Virtual WAN, it collects hub router traffic volume metrics continuously and supports alerts for routing anomalies. It is widely used to continuously monitor performance, detect anomalies and failures, respond to events affecting reliability, and is also accessed by agent personas such as the Production Monitoring Agent for load testing and monitoring purposes.<SEP>Azure Monitor is the underlying Azure infrastructure used by Azure Monitor for SAP solutions.<SEP>Azure Monitor provides diagnostic logs and metrics for cluster health visibility and operational dashboards.<SEP>Azure Monitor provides monitoring capabilities for HPC deployments and cluster reliability.

Azure CNI (Azure Container Networking Interface) is a network plugin that integrates AKS clusters within virtual networks by assigning IP addresses from the same virtual network to nodes, pods, and services. It supports a richer feature set compared to alternatives and enables Azure or Calico network policies for traffic control within AKS clusters. Azure CNI is robust, scalable, and recommended for most AKS scenarios. It is required for specific scenarios such as Windows-based node pools and Kubernetes network policies.

Azure App Service is a Microsoft Azure Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) product that provides a fully managed, low-friction container platform for building, deploying, hosting, and scaling web applications, APIs, and application workloads. It serves as an alternative to both Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and traditional IIS server setups, supporting multiple web apps and APIs on a single App Service plan. It is also a hosting platform option for deploying models and provides the underlying compute infrastructure for Azure Functions deployments.

Azure App Service offers extensive built-in capabilities including deployment slots that enable deploying live apps with their own host names, supporting gradual rollouts by swapping between slots after deployment. It provides Health Checks for scale-out operations, automatic scaling, integration with Azure Monitor Autoscale, and disaster recovery and backup features. The service supports zone-redundant deployments across availability zones for high availability of consumer applications, FTP deployments, remote debugging via Kudu, and profiling, memory dump collection, analysis, and autohealing features for .NET and Java apps. IPv6 support considerations also apply to its Web Apps feature.

The service operates as a multitenant environment where each instance has a limited number of outbound ports available and can be configured to run multiple instances. It is referenced for troubleshooting intermittent outbound connection errors using connection pooling and as an example for disabling unused ports and protocols during network hardening practices. It can be deployed via virtual network injection and integrates with other Azure services.

Azure App Service includes the Web Apps feature for hosting web application deployments and the WebJob feature for background task execution. It is recommended for low-latency scenarios when hosting web APIs. In practical applications, it is used to host e-commerce websites, as demonstrated in FMA examples with zone-redundant configurations.<SEP>Azure App Service is a PaaS compute platform designed for hosting web applications.<SEP>Azure App Service is a PaaS service that allows direct integration with other PaaS services without deploying virtual networks.
Prometheus metrics integration is supported via Azure Monitor's container insights.

SNAT port exhaustion is a common failure scenario in App Service involving outbound connections to public IP addresses.<SEP>SNAT port exhaustion occurs when a large number of outbound requests depletes available source NAT ports, preventing new outbound connections.<SEP>SNAT port exhaustion is a reliability event that can occur on an egress firewall when security tooling limitations are not accounted for.<SEP>SNAT port exhaustion occurs when a large number of outbound requests depletes available source NAT ports, preventing new outbound connections.<SEP>SNAT port exhaustion is a reliability event that can occur on an egress firewall when security tooling limitations are not accounted for.<SEP>SNAT port exhaustion is a potential issue with outbound traffic that can be mitigated using Azure NAT Gateway or Load Balancer.<SEP>SNAT port exhaustion occurs in multitenant applications when distinct network connections per tenant exhaust available source network address translation ports.

Calico is a network policy option enabled through Azure CNI for controlling traffic within AKS clusters.<SEP>A network policy plugin for AKS with a richer feature set including support for Windows nodes and both Azure CNI and Kubenet.<SEP>Calico is a network policy implementation prioritized for its richer feature set and broader community support.<SEP>A network policy plugin for AKS with a richer feature set including support for Windows nodes and both Azure CNI and Kubenet.<SEP>Calico is a network policy implementation prioritized for its richer feature set and broader community support.<SEP>Calico is a network policy tool providing capabilities including policy ordering, priority, deny rules, and flexible match rules.

Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform used for managing containerized applications. It provides features such as Network Policy for defining traffic rules between pods, secrets management (injecting secrets as environment variables into deployments), and logical segmentation of flows. Kubernetes enhances performance and scalability as a container orchestrator.

Kubernetes serves as the foundation upon which Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is built, with regular version releases. Its desired state configuration can be managed by GitOps tools like Flux. Kubernetes is also used as an example application stack with medium-touch and high-touch Infrastructure as Code (IaC) layers.<SEP>Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform managed using GitOps solutions like Flux.<SEP>Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform that AKS manages as a service.<SEP>Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform that AKS is built upon, providing scheduling and cluster management capabilities.<SEP>Kubernetes is a self-hosting option that provides more predictable latency behavior for inferencing.

Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a managed Kubernetes container orchestration service provided by Microsoft Azure that enables quick cluster provisioning with advanced networking, identity, and reliability features. It serves as a platform for deploying and managing containerized applications with high availability, scalability, and portability, commonly used in baseline mission-critical architectures for running microservices.

AKS supports a broad range of capabilities including network policies, node pools, multiple networking models, separate pod deployments on each node with updatable service definitions, and zone-redundant deployments across availability zones. As an Azure PaaS product, it offers multi-region best practices, backup capabilities, HTTP proxy support, custom certificate authority integration, and Azure CNI static block allocation. Pod CPU and memory limits can be defined to optimize performance, and it supports event-driven autoscaling via KEDA, horizontal pod automatic scaling, and cluster automatic scaling via Azure Monitor. AKS also supports resource density through namespaces and node pools, and provides configurable control plane and data plane logs.

AKS clusters host application services that use workload identities to authenticate to other components. The service requires regular Kubernetes version updates, providing a 90-day window to opt in before updates become automatic. It integrates with Container Apps for advanced networking and monitoring, and can be protected using Azure Firewall. AKS is also referenced as an example for blue-green deployment architecture.

Beyond general-purpose container orchestration, AKS serves as a model serving layer for hosting AI and machine learning inferencing workloads. It can be attached to Azure Machine Learning for self-hosting models and supports hosting deployed machine learning models with availability zone support. Additionally, AKS is a resource type that can be deployed on Azure Local, extending its reach to hybrid and edge environments.<SEP>Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) hosts custom processing logic and offers stronger reliability than Azure Logic Apps.<SEP>Azure Kubernetes Service is a cloud platform used for hosting inference servers with node pool isolation capabilities.<SEP>Azure Kubernetes Service is a platform that can host inference servers and other workloads on Azure.<SEP>Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a hosting compute platform that can influence workflow orchestrator choice.<SEP>Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a general-purpose compute platform that can host web apps, AI workloads, and batch compute tasks.<SEP>Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is an Azure service that should not be directly exposed to the internet without WAF protection.

Azure Container Apps is an Azure PaaS product and container management platform that enables building serverless microservices based on containers, powered by Kubernetes and open-source technologies. It is recommended as a first choice for container management depending on requirements.

Azure Container Apps supports event-driven autoscaling via KEDA and provides disaster recovery capabilities. The service includes environments owned by workload teams to run business logic for applications. Microsoft provides key recommendations and design checklists for Azure Container Apps covering security, performance, and cost optimization.<SEP>Azure Container Apps is a fully managed serverless container service that runs microservices and containerized applications on Azure, with built-in autoscaling and support for multiple languages and frameworks.<SEP>Azure Container Apps is a cloud service for running containerized applications with built-in observability, scaling, and security features.<SEP>Azure Container Apps is a cloud service for running containerized applications with various security and networking configurations.<SEP>Azure Container Apps is a service that can automatically scale based on queue depth and processing demand.<SEP>Azure Container Apps is a hosting platform option for deploying models.<SEP>Azure Container Apps is a PaaS compute platform for easy management of containerized applications.

Azure Virtual Machines use managed disks for storage and support encryption of virtual disk files to prevent unauthorized access. They can host application deployments and support automatic scaling. Mission-Critical Workloads are applications and systems that require the highest levels of reliability, availability, fault tolerance, and performance. They are significant in scale and complexity, and their architecture varies based on business requirements and acceptable downtime levels.

On Azure, mission-critical workloads are designed to maximize reliability, with baseline architectures recommending containerization and container orchestrators for application deployment. For the highest reliability, these workloads should leverage both multiple availability zones and multiple regions.

Mission-critical workloads prioritize real-time monitoring dashboards that site reliability engineers can quickly act on to maintain performance and availability.<SEP>Mission-critical workloads are systems that should use both multiple availability zones and multiple regions for the highest reliability.<SEP>Workloads requiring high reliability with design methodology focused on zero-downtime deployments and fast failure recovery.

Azure Marketplace is a platform for publishing, distributing, and acquiring a wide range of solutions and resources for use within the Azure ecosystem. It provides standard and trusted images for virtual machine and Azure Virtual Desktop deployments, including hardened images from CIS. Azure Marketplace offers partner firewall and web application firewall vendor products, as well as third-party queues and tools that can be integrated with Azure services to support asynchronous operations. It also serves as a platform for publishing and distributing SaaS solutions, providing support for billing, onboarding, offboarding, and customer access management, including management of billing for solutions deployed into customer environments.<SEP>Azure Marketplace provides supported base images with the latest updates for use in golden image creation.<SEP>Azure Marketplace hosts certified third-party backup solutions for SAP workloads.

Azure Functions is a serverless compute platform provided by Microsoft Azure that enables event-driven execution of application logic as distinct functions in response to events. It is designed for short-duration, event-driven triggers, making it suitable for background jobs, scheduled tasks via timer triggers, processing messages from queues or topics, and building orchestration with minimal code. It is positioned as a low-code/no-code tool for building serverless applications.

Azure Functions supports various deployment and reliability features, including zone-redundant deployments, virtual network injection, and multiple hosting plans with networking options. It offers Premium and Dedicated plans for autoscaling consumer applications based on incoming events, with concurrency support and the ability to bind to the change feed processor for custom backups. It is associated with App Service and features updated architecture best practices.

The service integrates with monitoring and observability tools, supporting autoinstrumentation sampling configuration for Application Insights monitoring, configurable log levels, and scope. It is central to workload design recommendations covering operational excellence, performance efficiency, security, and monitoring.

Azure Functions plays a key role in event-driven architectures, handling events and using managed identities for authentication with Event Grid. It can automate scaling responses based on Event Grid metrics and serves as a dependency that can affect event processing. It works with Azure Service Bus for planned traffic message processing and manages partitions automatically as a downstream consumer for Event Hubs. It can also configure auto-start triggers and adjust throughput units based on alert triggers for automated cost optimization.

Azure Functions serves as a key automation resource, enabling organizations to automate tasks including incident response, remediation actions, and self-healing workflows such as restarting failed jobs or scaling clusters.<SEP>Azure Functions is a service evaluated for Service Bus workflow automation capabilities.<SEP>Azure Functions is a serverless compute service used for automating Service Bus operational tasks.<SEP>Azure Functions handles operations requiring Azure Resource Manager interaction.<SEP>Azure Functions is an Azure native tool that can forward logs by creating listeners for incoming logs from Azure VMware Solution.

Azure Logic Apps is a serverless, low-code, cloud-based platform within Microsoft Azure for creating and running automated workflows that integrate apps, data, services, and systems. It provides a visual designer (graphical user interface) and supports configuration files for building orchestration across multiple services and systems. The platform offers a library of built-in connectors and templates, enabling users to integrate various services without extensive coding.

Azure Logic Apps supports stateful workflows and can run timers to regularly send requests to APIs or web services, making it suitable for schedule-driven background job invocation and orchestration tasks. It creates new application versions on updates and maintains version history, allowing for rollback or promotion of previous versions.

Azure Logic Apps is associated with Azure App Service and serves numerous practical use cases, including building self-healing workflows that automatically respond to problems in Azure Databricks operations, automating scaling responses based on Event Grid metrics, processing Azure Advisor recommendations automatically for cost optimization, and exporting tables not supported by data export to protect data.<SEP>Azure Logic Apps is a service evaluated for Service Bus workflow automation capabilities.<SEP>Azure Logic Apps is a workflow automation service used for operational tasks like dead letter queue cleanup and subscription maintenance.<SEP>Azure Logic Apps is a simpler tool suitable for smaller data workloads.<SEP>Azure Logic Apps is an Azure native tool that can be used to create listeners for incoming logs and forward them to storage.<SEP>Azure Logic Apps is used for building workflows in IT service management solutions.

Azure API Management is an Azure PaaS solution for publishing, transforming, monitoring, and proxying APIs across all environments, including hybrid and multicloud. It serves as an API gateway that exposes APIs to external clients or different application teams while minimizing network access to back-end APIs.

The service offers multiple deployment options and tiers, including a Consumption tier and a Premium v2 tier, along with various scaling options and workspaces. It supports deployment via virtual network injection and is considered for application delivery capabilities.

Azure API Management provides built-in policies for rate limiting and supports advanced request throttling. It includes built-in caching capabilities and can be used for API mocking, acting as a facade to back-end services. The service has received refactored guidance for improved clarity and usability.<SEP>Azure API Management is a service used alongside Application Gateway to protect APIs.<SEP>Azure API Management is a feature-rich application gateway that helps securely publish, manage, and monitor APIs deployed to Service Fabric clusters.<SEP>Azure API Management is a platform used to implement AI gateways.<SEP>Azure API Management helps securely publish API endpoints and manage API methods and behaviors, including security policies for authentication and authorization.<SEP>Azure API Management is a service that provides request throttling and caching capabilities to improve API efficiency.<SEP>Azure API Management is a service with multiple tiers including Premium and consumption, where choosing higher tiers may lead to unused resources.

Power Automate is a low-code/no-code tool for workflow automation with integrations configurable through connections.<SEP>Power Automate is a Microsoft product listed as a related automation resource.<SEP>Power Automate is a workflow automation tool used for managing incident response and retrospective workflows.

Serverless computing provides on-demand resources, eliminating infrastructure management, with automatic provisioning and scaling.<SEP>Serverless computing is a technique for optimizing architecture and achieving better resource utilization and cost efficiency.
Image locking prevents changes or deletions to container image versions or repositories in Container Registry.

Zone Redundancy is a built-in Azure reliability feature that distributes resources, replicas, and instances across multiple availability zones within a region to enhance availability and resilience. It ensures that workloads can withstand failures in a single availability zone by enabling automatic failover to remaining zones, providing protection against datacenter outages.

Zone Redundancy applies across multiple Azure services. For Azure App Service, it allows applications to withstand single-zone failures by provisioning instances across multiple zones. For Azure Load Balancer, it distributes traffic across zones to handle availability zone failures. For Premium tier Azure Container Registry, it provides protection against availability zone failure. As a general Azure reliability feature, it offers immediate resilience improvements by spreading instances across multiple datacenters and deploying units across multiple availability zones within a region.<SEP>Zone redundancy eliminates single points of failure within regional infrastructure with automatic failover during zone failures.<SEP>Zone redundancy distributes compute and storage across multiple Azure availability zones for resilience against zone outages.<SEP>Zone redundancy distributes replicas across availability zones to eliminate single points of failure within a region.<SEP>Zone redundancy provides datacenter failure protection with higher SLA guarantees by eliminating availability zones as single points of failure.
