Azure Application Gateway is a regional, managed Azure service that functions as a web traffic load balancer and application delivery controller, specifically designed for HTTP/HTTPS applications. It serves as an alternative to Azure Load Balancer, providing features such as TLS/SSL termination, URL-based routing, session affinity, health probes for monitoring backend availability, and the ability to choose TLS versions and cipher suites.

From a security perspective, Azure Application Gateway includes integrated Web Application Firewall (WAF) capabilities that scan for and block OWASP attack types, securing HTTP/HTTPS traffic. It provides network isolation and traffic filtering within regional deployment stamps, IDPS capabilities, and can integrate with Azure Web Application Firewall for additional protection. WAF events can be analyzed through Security Copilot integration.

Azure Application Gateway supports flexible traffic management through listeners and URL path-based routing, enabling density across deployments. It can distribute traffic across stamps in single-zone deployments and supports routing for hybrid and on-premises services. The service is used in various Azure deployment architectures, including AI workload deployments, serving as an Azure-native networking device for inbound traffic control and application traffic management.

Client-side logic that handles failover scenarios when the primary global routing technology fails, routing to redundant technology.<SEP>Client-side logic that handles failover scenarios when the primary global routing technology fails, routing to redundant technology.

Session Affinity, also known as session stickiness, is a mechanism that routes requests from the same client or source to the same backend server or origin. It typically uses client-side cookies to ensure that subsequent requests are directed to the same backend that handled the first request, maintaining state continuity across a user's session.

While Session Affinity can be useful for maintaining session state, it has several drawbacks. It ties requests to specific backends, which can negatively impact traffic distribution balance and cause overloading on a single origin server. It also limits scaling ability and introduces single points of failure. For these reasons, Session Affinity is not recommended for stateless applications or from a reliability perspective, as it reduces load balancing flexibility.

TLS, or Transport Layer Security, is the industry standard encryption protocol for securing network connections by encrypting and authenticating data in transit between clients and servers. It ensures confidentiality and integrity of data exchange across networks, standardizing secure communication for protocols such as HTTPS. TLS 1.2 is widely cited as the recommended minimum version for secure client-server communication, while TLS 1.3 is recognized as the latest and most secure version.

In Azure environments, TLS is managed via services such as Azure Front Door's managed certificate service and Application Gateway, providing end-to-end encryption and secure connections. TLS handles encrypted connections from TLS offloading points to application backends and supports traffic isolation in classified data flows for sensitive environments. As part of network transformation, TLS can be turned off and reestablished at different hops with more rigorously managed certificates to meet evolving security requirements.

X-Azure-FDID is a header used for filtering and validating that incoming requests flow through the configured Azure Front Door instance.<SEP>X-Azure-FDID is a header used for filtering and validating that incoming requests flow through the configured Azure Front Door instance.

A regional deployment stamp is an independent deployment unit within a region that can be taken out of circulation if dependencies become unhealthy.<SEP>A regional deployment stamp is an independent deployment unit within a region that can be taken out of circulation if dependencies become unhealthy.

Virtual Network is a fundamental networking construct in Azure that enables private connectivity between resources. It provides a logical boundary for network isolation, where by design one virtual network cannot communicate with another unless intentionally connected through mechanisms such as peering. Virtual networks are used to segment and isolate workload components using subnets, supporting various network configurations.

Virtual networks enable organizations to move to private IP address spaces and minimize network line of sight, enhancing security. They can be used to control both outbound and inbound traffic for services such as App Service, enabling network isolation and security. When planning address spaces, they should be kept large enough to support future scaling needs.<SEP>Virtual networks are Azure networking resources used as boundaries for network segmentation between customers, supporting peering and isolation.

Azure Firewall is a cloud-native, fully stateful, managed Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) network security service in Microsoft Azure that provides centralized firewall protection for Azure workloads. It filters traffic between cloud resources, the internet, and on-premises networks, supporting both east-west and north-south traffic inspection. It operates as a network edge firewall, typically deployed in centralized hub network models for egress control, requiring a dedicated subnet and available as either a dedicated or centrally shared resource across customers.

Azure Firewall offers layer 3 through layer 7 controls, including NAT, network, and application rules, FQDN filtering (including SQL FQDNs), DNAT with FQDN filtering, IDPS/IDS capabilities, DNS proxy, threat intelligence, and optional TLS inspection/termination for HTTP/HTTPS traffic. It analyzes traffic and blocks connections to untrusted destinations, enabling organizations to filter, restrict, and inspect both outbound and inbound traffic from resources such as Virtual Machines and container environments. It also provides added security for routing traffic through internal load balancers for non-HTTP applications.

Azure Firewall is available in multiple SKUs—Basic, Standard, and Premium—each offering varying feature sets. Advanced capabilities include forced tunneling for egress traffic control, port exhaustion and SNAT exhaustion mitigation, explicit proxy configuration, hierarchical policy rules, packet capture, DNS flow trace logs, and data transformation before log storage. It provides Resource Health monitoring, customer-controlled maintenance schedules, change tracking, diagnostic logs, policy analytics, and network infrastructure automation, supporting scaling up to 20 instances for high availability. It is charged per instance and can be expensive, making centralized shared deployments a common cost optimization pattern.

Azure Firewall integrates with numerous Azure services and architectures. It works with Application Gateway for virtual network protection, Azure Databricks via virtual network injection, Azure Policy for governance, and Microsoft Sentinel via a dedicated data connector. It serves as an egress point for AKS cluster node pools, controlling cluster egress traffic and enforcing security policies. It is deployed in Azure Virtual WAN virtual hubs for centralized application-aware filtering, threat protection, and security inspection. Azure Firewall also provides east-west and north-south protection and filtering for Azure Virtual Desktop workloads, helping lock down and secure session host environments. It is used in multiregion load balancing architectures as a key component for traffic inspection, control, and network egress across various Azure networking scenarios.<SEP>Azure Firewall is a network security device deployed in Azure for monitoring and filtering traffic.<SEP>Azure Firewall is used to inspect Azure VMware Solution traffic to the internet and Azure for internet-facing workloads.<SEP>Azure Firewall is an Azure service used for intrusion detection and prevention in network traffic.<SEP>Azure Firewall protects internet-facing workloads by creating separation between endpoints.

Virtual WAN is an Azure networking service that provides hub-based connectivity infrastructure for wide-area network architectures. It supports hub-and-spoke network topologies with features including VPN gateways (such as S2S VPN), ExpressRoute gateways, hub routers, and comprehensive routing capabilities including routing intent and policies for traffic redirection.

Virtual WAN offers connectivity, security, routing, and monitoring capabilities, along with cost optimization and multiregion architecture support. It serves as a network topology option for deploying and managing Azure Firewall instances, and Azure Firewall Manager can centrally manage these instances within the Virtual WAN environment through secure hubs. Virtual WAN supports sharing Azure Firewall instances across hubs, though Azure DDoS Protection plan association via Firewall Manager does not apply to it.

The service has specific exceptions for forced tunneling and private data plane configurations. Performance indicators, capacity planning, and monitoring practices are defined for Virtual WAN to ensure optimal operation.

Firewall Manager is an Azure security management service that provides centralized deployment and management of Azure Firewall instances and their associated policies through global firewall policies. It enables administrators to configure security partner providers, create and associate Azure DDoS Protection plans with hub virtual networks, and manage firewall policies from a single point of control. Pricing for Firewall Manager is based on firewall associations.

An Availability Zone is a physically separate and isolated datacenter location within an Azure region, designed to provide high availability, fault isolation, and resiliency against outages. Each Availability Zone consists of one or more datacenters equipped with independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure, ensuring that a failure in one zone does not affect others. Inter-zone latency within a region is guaranteed to be sub-2ms. Availability Zones are used for deploying resources with redundancy and resiliency considerations, enabling organizations to protect their applications and data from datacenter-level failures.<SEP>An availability zone is a deployment option for session hosts to improve reliability.<SEP>An availability zone is a deployment option for session hosts to protect them from failures in specific fault domains.

Private Link is an Azure networking feature that enables direct service-to-service communication using private endpoints within or across regions. It provides a way to give a PaaS instance a private IP address, making it unreachable over the public internet, thereby eliminating public internet exposure and ensuring that management traffic remains within the Azure backbone network.

Network Security Groups (NSGs) are Azure resources that function as Layer 3 and Layer 4 firewalls, filtering and controlling network traffic between resources in virtual networks and external networks. They are applied at the subnet or network interface (NIC) level, acting as perimeter traffic filters that use IP-based access control lists (ACLs) to secure ingress paths based on IP addresses, ports, and protocols. NSGs enable micro-segmentation of application traffic and enforcement of security rules on subnets.

NSGs are widely used across Azure services. They control traffic flow in Azure Databricks virtual network configurations, create micro-segmentation for Event Grid network boundaries, limit access for Azure NetApp Files, filter traffic to back-end servers, provide additional filtering for subnets containing Service Bus consumers and producers, and restrict traffic flow between subnets and node types in Service Fabric clusters. They also control traffic to and from Azure Cosmos DB resources, manage SQL Managed Instance subnet traffic (with unique assignment per subnet), provide subnet-level filtering in spoke networks, and support network-level segmentation for services such as App Service. NSGs serve as an alternative to Azure Firewall for intra-virtual network traffic control, restrict access to private endpoint IP addresses, manage access control in virtual network peering scenarios, and control access to databases as part of the Zero Trust security model's network segmentation strategy.<SEP>Network Security Groups (NSGs) are used to segment and isolate subnets and workloads by controlling traffic flow.<SEP>Network Security Groups (NSGs) are used to configure network rules based on least-privilege access principles.<SEP>Network security groups filter network traffic to and from Azure Virtual Desktop workloads using service tags and rules.<SEP>Network Security Groups filter network traffic at the source to eliminate unnecessary data transmission.<SEP>Azure feature used to filter network traffic at the source, reducing unnecessary data transmission.<SEP>NSGs filter network traffic to and from SAP workloads by defining allow/deny rules.

Zero Trust is a security model, strategy, and guiding principle that assumes a breached state and eliminates implicit trust across all layers of an application and network. It treats all processes, operations, and network requests—including internal traffic—as potential attack vectors, enforcing explicit, continuous verification of all available data points.

Core principles of Zero Trust include explicit verification, least-privilege access, defense in depth, and deny-by-default access controls. By defaulting to no access and introducing only the minimum permissions necessary, Zero Trust minimizes the attack surface, limits lateral movement, and reduces the blast radius of potential breaches. Network segmentation restricts communication paths between components to only what is needed, with strict access policies governing traffic between workloads. Traffic analytics support these segmentation boundaries by monitoring flows, enforcing policies, and detecting anomalous activity.

Microsoft promotes Zero Trust as a proactive, integrated security approach applied across all layers, including Azure Firewall and Application Gateway configurations. Its guiding principles also serve as a framework for organizing firewall rules and security policies, ensuring that network rule configuration follows least-privilege access practices and that all traffic—both external and internal—is controlled and inspected.<SEP>Zero Trust is a security framework with principles like verify explicitly and least-privileged access.

Azure RBAC (Azure Role-Based Access Control) is the authorization system that manages access to Azure resources by assigning permissions to users, groups, and applications based on roles at defined scopes, including subscription, resource group, or individual resource levels. It represents security principals in Microsoft Entra ID and supports the principle of least privileged access, restricting the actions that authorized users can perform to mitigate risks such as compromised tokens or keys.

Azure RBAC supports segmentation by isolating access by job function, allowing only certain actions for certain roles and scopes. It provides both built-in and customizable roles across various Azure services. For example, it offers roles like Data Sender, Data Receiver, and Data Owner for messaging operations, grants workspace permissions to administrators, controls access to Event Grid resources, and serves as an authentication and authorization method in Service Bus security configuration. It is also used to manage access to Azure Databricks components through Microsoft Entra ID integration and to grant users access to SAP workload resources.

Beyond access management, Azure RBAC restricts management operations, applies resource locks, and enforces security configurations through Azure Policy, providing centralized control over the Azure control plane and resources.<SEP>Azure Role-Based Access Control enforces least-privilege access across HPC resources.

nodes.description:
Azure Key Vault is a secure secret, key, and certificate management service provided by Microsoft Azure. It serves as a hardened repository for managing application secrets such as passwords, connection strings, API keys, database credentials, authentication tokens, preshared keys (including Redis and third-party secrets), certificates (including TLS/SSL certificates), and cryptographic keys—all stored outside of source code in an encrypted environment with audit capabilities.

The service offers features including expiry settings, key rotation policies, seamless certificate and secret rotation to minimize performance effects, alerting for upcoming expirations, access audit logging, and secure access control through Azure RBAC and access policies for identity-based management. It stores certificates with extensions that automatically refresh them when changes are detected. It provides high availability through automatic redundancy across multiple regions, operating as a global Azure service with HSM backing, transaction limits, and a defined security boundary.

Azure Key Vault is commonly used as a typical internal dependency in cloud workloads, playing a critical role in scaling operations and overall availability. It stores customer-managed keys and secrets, manages credentials required by workloads to access services such as Blob Storage, Azure Files, and Event Hubs, and supports customer-managed key encryption of data at rest, including cross-tenant scenarios. It integrates with services like Azure Databricks for secret scopes, Azure App Configuration for secure application configuration management, and Azure Virtual Desktop as a security service. The service is a Microsoft Entra protected resource, accessible via mechanisms such as AKS Workload IDs, and is also accessed by the Discriminative AI Data Scientist as a component.

Azure Key Vault serves important roles in database security, providing unified life cycle management for TDE (Transparent Data Encryption) protectors and Always Encrypted column master keys with audit logging. It backs up TDE encryption keys for customer-managed key scenarios, protects credentials and encryption keys for SQL Managed Instance, manages certificates for Service Fabric clusters, and enables centralized management of encryption keys within dedicated instances to prevent accidental key loss.

Azure Key Vault is a recommended technology for security and access control, and a recommended approach for storing secrets needed in automated deployment processes. Beyond cloud application secrets, it serves as a secure external location for storing BitLocker recovery keys. Its centralized storage for secrets, encryption keys, and access credentials—combined with support for regular rotation, audit logging, and robust access policies—makes it an essential component of cloud infrastructure for secure management of sensitive materials.<SEP>Azure Key Vault is a service used for key management, secret storage, and encryption operations in Azure VMware Solution.<SEP>Azure Key Vault is a security service integrated with Azure VMware Solution.<SEP>Azure Key Vault is a service used to securely store encryption keys.<SEP>Azure Key Vault stores application secrets, customer-managed keys, and supports database encryption.

Managed Identities are identities for Azure resources managed by Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory). They allow Azure resources—including App Service instances, Container Apps, Function Apps, and AKS clusters—to authenticate to other services supporting Microsoft Entra authentication without storing secrets, managing service principal credentials, or handling credentials directly. By enabling applications to authenticate via an identity provider, managed identities help minimize the risk of credential leakage and theft.

Managed Identities automatically rotate and protect credentials, eliminating the need for manual credentials management. They remove credential management overhead for service-to-service communication patterns, application-to-instance connectivity, cross-service integrations, and database access (eliminating the need for database keys or credentials). They are favored over hard-coded secrets and are recommended as the instance identity for Azure service integration.

Managed Identities are classified as nonhuman identities and can replace human access to processes such as deployments and database changes. As non-human accounts within Identity and Access Management (IAM), they often have incorrect permissions and should be included in permissions audits to ensure proper security governance. They are recommended for automated authentication in production workloads to maintain security.

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is a security method for regulating access to resources based on roles assigned to users. It follows the principle of least privilege, controlling what actions authorized users can perform and managing permissions across various contexts including Azure resources, identity components, and secret management systems.

RBAC is applied in production CD pipelines to mitigate security risks and in DevOps tooling to manage service principal access. It grants access to manage resources within segments through role assignments, ensuring role-specific visibility with appropriate security controls. RBAC can be enhanced with conditions based on context, actions, and attributes for more granular permission management. It is also used with Microsoft Entra ID to create logical access control boundaries for identity-based segmentation, such as in Event Hubs.

RBAC enforces separation between development, testing, and production environments through access control policies. It restricts access to Application Gateway's control plane to authorized identities only, limits who can create, resize, or configure database servers, and restricts access to credentials. RBAC is used to block actions that can lead to overspending on storage resources and is included in extended deployment templates for MySQL flexible server.

RBAC serves as an access control mechanism in AKS authentication and configuration policies, assigns least-privilege access roles for Event Grid operations, delegates permissions with built-in roles for platform administrators and workload operators, limits access for operations on Azure NetApp Files through custom roles, and manages workspace access permissions using the principle of least privilege.<SEP>Role-based access control (RBAC) controls who can modify Virtual WAN configuration using built-in or custom roles.<SEP>Role-based access control assigns permissions like Network Contributor and Reader roles to prevent unauthorized configuration changes.<SEP>RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is used to block actions that can lead to overspending as part of cost guardrails.<SEP>Role-based access control (RBAC) is a system for managing authorization based on user roles.<SEP>Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) delegation schema implements least-privilege access using built-in Azure Virtual Desktop roles.<SEP>Role-based access control assigns roles and permissions based on the principle of least privilege to control access to workloads.

nodes.description:
Microsoft Defender for Cloud, formerly known as Azure Security Center, is a comprehensive security monitoring, management, and governance service available on Azure. It functions as a security information and event management (SIEM) solution and cloud workload protection platform (CWPP), typically enabled for subscriptions containing mission-critical workload resources. It is also a default security feature included in Azure Local.

The platform provides built-in threat detection capabilities, analyzing logs, checking compromised IP addresses, and offering vulnerability scanning across various technology areas. It receives telemetry data and logs from Azure Monitor Agent to power its security insights. Microsoft Defender for Cloud triggers alerts when anomalies in activity occur, notifies administrators, and routes security detection alerts to security operations teams. It also sends Azure incident notifications to designated points of contact.

Microsoft Defender for Cloud discovers misconfigurations in Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and delivers workload protection solutions including network recommendations. Threat Modeling is a structured, proactive engineering discipline and design practice used to identify, evaluate, and mitigate potential security threats to a system. It provides a risk-based approach to security design by systematically analyzing potential threats, attacks, vulnerabilities, and attack vectors that may affect a workload or application.

As a method, Threat Modeling produces reports of attack vectors prioritized by severity, enabling teams to develop appropriate security mitigations and countermeasures. It is applied early in the design phase to identify vulnerabilities and build hardening plans before they can be exploited. The practice extends beyond initial design to encompass code review and deployment pipelines, ensuring threats are identified throughout the development lifecycle.

Threat Modeling serves as a key component of maturing security practices within organizations, functioning as both an intensive exercise for building mitigation plans and a requirement for comprehensive security coverage across systems and processes.<SEP>Threat modeling is an exercise that points to key areas to ensure test coverage and frequency.

Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is a key reliability and disaster recovery metric that defines the maximum acceptable amount of downtime before services, systems, applications, or workloads must be restored after a disruption or outage. It serves as a target for how quickly recovery procedures must be completed, establishing the tolerable window of time between a failure event and the resumption of normal operations.

RTO is determined through failure mode analysis and disaster recovery planning processes. It applies to individual systems, applications, and operational flows, guiding organizations in designing their resilience strategies and ensuring that restoration efforts meet defined business continuity requirements.

RTO is also used as a practical benchmark in operational testing and validation. It is verified through incident response testing and restore drills to ensure recovery performance meets defined targets. Additionally, RTO serves as a criterion in failback data synchronization processes, ensuring that data recovery and system restoration align with acceptable downtime tolerances.<SEP>Recovery Time Objective, the target time for restoring a solution after an outage.<SEP>Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is a metric used to determine the appropriate redundancy level for data storage.<SEP>Recovery Time Objective defines the maximum acceptable downtime for recovery after a failure.

nodes.description:
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is a reliability and recovery metric that defines the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time during a disruption. It represents the threshold for how much data an organization can afford to lose, applicable to individual systems, applications, and data flows.

RPO is determined through failure mode analysis and disaster recovery planning, and is directly controlled by backup frequency—more frequent backups result in a lower RPO and less potential data loss. It is also used to determine the appropriate redundancy level for data storage. As a key recovery metric, RPO is used to define recovery targets for workloads and to validate data integrity during recovery. It is verified through incident response testing to ensure systems meet their defined objectives.

nodes.description:
Service Level Objective (SLO) is a measurable, agreed-upon target for service reliability that defines the desired level of service along with specific quality attributes. SLOs serve as critical health signals for applications, setting targets for critical flows such as availability and response time. For example, an SLO might target 99.45% availability or specify response time thresholds at the 75th percentile for an API, with some targeting criteria as stringent as 99.999% uptime.

SLOs should be achievable and clearly communicated. They can be composite values calculated from multiple contributing factors. SLOs are used to evaluate whether potential downtime falls within tolerable limits and serve as the basis for calculating error budgets, enabling teams to balance reliability with development velocity.<SEP>Service Level Objectives are critical health signals that define the desired level of service along with quality attributes.

Chaos Engineering is a discipline and practice centered on deliberately injecting faults, failures, and real-world stresses into systems to test their resilience, improve reliability, and validate recoverability. It involves conducting controlled experiments—often in production environments, though also in nonproduction environments—to confirm that applications and services can recover gracefully under adverse conditions. Through active malfunction simulation and load testing, Chaos Engineering helps teams build confidence in system robustness, test incident response processes, and validate event processing resilience during simulated infrastructure failures.

Considered a gold standard for resilience validation, Chaos Engineering is typically reserved for mature systems that have safeguards in place to limit the blast radius of experiments. By proactively subjecting infrastructure to realistic failure scenarios, organizations can systematically identify resilience gaps and weaknesses, validate mitigation and recovery procedures, and prevent unexpected outages. It is widely used to measure, understand, and improve cloud application and service resilience.<SEP>Chaos engineering is a testing approach to identify points of failure before outages occur.<SEP>Chaos engineering is a testing method that introduces faults to improve workload reliability, resilience, and fault handling while considering sustainability impacts.

Failover is the process of switching operations from a primary environment to a secondary or standby system when the primary becomes unavailable due to a failure or disaster. It involves the automated and/or manual shifting of production workload traffic from an unavailable region to an unaffected geographical region, ensuring continuity of service.

As a reliability technique, failover redirects work or data access to healthy components when malfunctions occur. It can be implemented through patterns such as Leader Election, Index Table, and Scheduler Agent Supervisor. For mission-critical workloads, automation of the failover process is recommended to minimize downtime and reduce the risk of human error.

Azure Backup is a cloud-based Azure service that provides comprehensive data protection through backup and restore operations across a wide range of Azure resources. It supports backup for virtual machines (including host-level and VM guest-level backups for Azure Local), Azure Files, SMB file shares, Azure Blob Storage, Azure Managed Disks, SQL Database, AKS clusters, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, and FSLogix profiles stored in Azure Files or Azure NetApp Files. It is also integrated with Azure VMware Solution.

Azure Backup uses incremental backups, compression, and encryption to minimize performance impact. It offers capabilities such as native database backup, storage backup, virtual machine backup, long-term retention (up to 99 years in Recovery Services vault), centralized backup management, soft delete, and recovery point management. For Azure Database for PostgreSQL, backup policies support recovery point retention up to 10 years. The service provides vaulted backup to protect data from threats such as ransomware attacks and offers geo-redundant backup capabilities.

For disaster recovery, Azure Backup vaults in a secondary region can protect persistent data without requiring standby infrastructure. It supports cross-region restores, stores recovery points in Backup vaults for AKS cluster disaster recovery, and provides centralized business continuity and disaster recovery management for services like SQL Database.

Azure Backup offers storage with reserved capacity, providing discounts for one-year or three-year commitments. For services like Azure Database for PostgreSQL, it incurs protected instance fees and backup storage fees. The service continues to receive new features enhancing disaster recovery guidance.<SEP>Azure Backup is the native backup solution in Azure providing database backups, storage backups, VM backups, long-term retention, and backup management for SAP workloads.<SEP>Azure Backup is a service that can take database backups for HANA and SQL Server.

The Deployment Stamps pattern is an architectural approach that creates repeatable, self-contained units (called stamps) containing all resources required to deliver a workload. This pattern shifts the focus from component-level to workload-level redundancy by bundling workload components into templates as units of scale, enabling easy and repeatable deployments.

The pattern is used to provision, manage, and monitor varied resources to host multiple workloads or tenants, with each copy referred to as a stamp. It is particularly suitable for multi-zone, multi-region deployments and is well-suited for SaaS providers. Critical Flows are essential workload paths and processes that are vital to primary business activities and operations. They represent the most important and high-priority workflows within a workload, typically characterized as business critical, time-sensitive, latency sensitive, and having a direct effect on revenue generation.

Critical Flows are assigned criticality levels based on multiple factors, including frequency, criticality, risk, data intensiveness, and architecture intensiveness. These classifications help determine the required components, resiliency approaches, and performance optimization strategies needed to support them.

Given their importance, Critical Flows require redundancy to meet reliability targets and must remain operational during outages. They demand prioritized resource allocation and performance optimization to ensure continuous operation and support of high-priority business processes.

Partitioning is the process of physically dividing data into separate data stores or smaller, manageable subsets. It is a data management and redesign strategy used to improve performance, scalability, and reliability, particularly as data growth occurs in production systems.

nodes.description: Assume Breach is a foundational security principle and Zero Trust concept that presupposes systems may already be compromised or that an attacker may eventually gain access. Latency refers to the time delay between when a request is initiated and when the result becomes available. It is a common response time metric, with example targets such as 200 milliseconds, and broadly measures the responsiveness of systems and operations.

In the context of networking and distributed systems, latency represents the time data takes to travel from source to destination, which increases the further services are from each other. Architectural components such as gateway routing, messaging brokers, and anti-corruption layers introduce additional latency that draws against performance target budgets.

In security contexts, latency is the delay added to requests by security controls such as inspection, identity verification, and encryption in workload flows. In storage systems, latency measures how long storage operations last, indicating the responsiveness of the storage system.

Capacity Planning is the process of forecasting workload demand and determining the resources required to meet that demand while balancing cost and performance. It involves proactively measuring, estimating, and provisioning computing resources—such as CPU, memory, storage, and network bandwidth—to address anticipated changes in capacity and meet workload performance targets.

Capacity Planning is an iterative process that shifts organizations from reactive to proactive resource management. Load Balancer is a networking service that distributes incoming traffic across multiple back-end instances to ensure reliability and availability. In Azure, Load Balancer operates as a Layer 4 network service supporting TCP and UDP traffic load balancing, though it does not support SSL/TLS termination. It is available in Basic and Standard SKUs and supports up to 5,000 VMs in a single back-end pool.

Load Balancer plays a critical role in autoscaling scenarios by distributing traffic across autoscaled replicas, requiring reliable operation. When built into zone-redundant services, it disperses requests across instances in multiple availability zones and redirects traffic during outages, enhancing fault tolerance.

Additionally, Load Balancer can serve as a global traffic management mechanism used to control traffic shifting between blue and green environments, supporting deployment strategies that minimize downtime.

Incident Management (also abbreviated as IcM) is a structured, cross-functional process for detecting, triaging, mitigating, and resolving production incidents—such as platform outages, data corruption, and performance degradation—within defined targets. It encompasses the full reactive lifecycle: receiving alerts, creating tickets, assigning them to appropriate teams, gathering context, correlating data, and performing initial triage to accelerate response times.

Beyond immediate response, Incident Management includes coordinating communication with customers and stakeholders, conducting post-incident retrospectives, and capturing lessons learned to prevent recurrence and improve overall system resilience. It involves observability design, role definition, infrastructure setup, and mitigation strategies as integral components.

Incident Management is typically provided as a skill by centralized operations teams handling workload disruptions across an organization. It also serves as a design area for establishing operational responsibilities, tools, and processes—particularly in SaaS workloads on platforms such as Azure—where organizational culture, processes, and tooling are key considerations.

The practice serves as a core prerequisite for effective disaster recovery planning. While inherently reactive, efficient monitoring aims to reduce reliance on Incident Management by anticipating issues before they affect customer experience.

Safe Deployment Practices (SDP) are processes, procedures, and strategies that define how to safely make and deploy changes to a workload, focusing on managing risk, minimizing human error, and keeping systems stable during routine, feature, and emergency updates in production. They serve as standards for integrating new functionality that ensure safe and proper operation of workloads.

SDP aim to achieve consistency in deployments using guardrails that reduce the effect of errors and unexpected conditions. They encompass a wide range of techniques including automation, Infrastructure as Code (IaC), branching strategies, feature flags, progressive exposure rollout, canary deployments, blue-green deployments, and dark launches to enhance flexibility and reliability. These practices often involve deploying multiple concurrent instances to shift traffic in a controlled way, which can increase resource costs but provides greater safety and control over the deployment process.

SDP include code promotion through environments and quality gate checks, which are followed even during emergency deployments albeit with accelerated timelines. They are enforced through CI/CD pipelines that prohibit manual deployment activities, ensuring consistency and repeatability. These practices also ensure safety around sensitive production data and align with zero-downtime requirements.

Additionally, Safe Deployment Practices apply to AI workloads, treating AI workload APIs the same as any other API by placing them behind a gateway and handling code with established deployment standards.<SEP>Safe deployment practices involve deploying updates progressively to customer groups using strategies like progressive exposure and health models.

Progressive exposure is a deployment strategy that involves the gradual rollout of new features or changes to successively larger groups of users, rather than releasing to all users simultaneously. This approach minimizes the potential blast radius of deployment-caused issues by controlling adoption in stages, allowing teams to uncover problems before broader rollout.

Progressive exposure can be implemented through various techniques, including feature flags, staged rollouts, canary releases, and side-by-side deployments. For example, canary releases target a small initial group of users first, enabling teams to monitor for issues and contain the impact of any vulnerabilities or defects before expanding to a wider audience. This controlled approach applies not only to traditional software changes but also to integrating models into production environments, making it a versatile risk-mitigation pattern across different deployment scenarios.<SEP>Progressive exposure is a deployment strategy that rolls out updates to customer groups in phases, starting with less-sensitive or early-adopter customers.

nodes.description:
Technical debt refers to the accumulated inefficiencies, suboptimal design choices, shortcuts, or deferred work taken during development to deliver code faster or meet deadlines. These less-than-ideal implementations go live and complicate maintenance over time, affecting overall system performance, maintainability, scalability, and slowing growth. It also encompasses the accumulated cost of maintaining underutilized or poorly designed features that hinder productivity, as well as drift from original design principles due to rapid iteration.

Technical debt accumulates when a lack of automation in system design promotes repetitive tasks, or when teams take shortcuts under time pressure. It represents the estimated future cost of addressing these known problems and accumulated code quality issues in a workload, requiring ongoing effort to resolve.

Beyond being a liability, technical debt can serve as a strategic tool in development—capturing short-term decisions and acting as a motivator for incremental updates. When incurred, it should be intentional, documented, and repayable. Workload teams should regularly address technical debt as a recurring backlog task, prioritizing and managing it to prevent compounding inefficiencies over time.<SEP>Technical debt refers to accepted risks and design shortcomings that require intentional decision-making, documentation, and proactive management by architects and workload teams.<SEP>Accumulated suboptimal technical decisions that architects systematically address through workload optimization.

nodes.description:
The Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) is a multistage, systematic process framework for developing software systems, spanning from ideation to delivery. It encompasses planning, design, development, testing, deployment, and monitoring activities, and can be implemented through various frameworks such as Scrum, Kanban, or Waterfall. The SDLC provides rigor, consistency, specificity, and prioritization to change management in a workload, reflecting industry-proven processes that enhance development efficiency.

The SDLC serves as the foundation into which baseline security practices and threat modeling should be integrated. Performance tests should also be conducted as early as possible within the SDLC to catch issues earlier. As architecture, business requirements, and team structure change, SDLC practices may need to evolve accordingly.

nodes.description:
Feature Flags are a software development technique that allows teams to control the visibility and behavior of features through conditional logic without requiring redeployment. They enable the selective enabling or disabling of new features in production, allowing controlled exposure to users and quick rollback if issues arise.

Feature Flags are commonly used in canary deployments, where new versions are enabled for target users to test changes incrementally. They also serve as a mechanism for gradually releasing changes to contain the impact of potential vulnerabilities. Overall, Feature Flags provide a practice for creating, changing, and deploying features in a controlled and safe manner.<SEP>Feature flags or runtime configuration properties are used to bypass problematic functionality during an incident.<SEP>Feature flags are a deployment technique used for orchestration code to control traffic and feature rollout.<SEP>Feature flags enable specific functionalities for certain users without customizing applications for individual customers.<SEP>Feature flags are used to enable specific functionalities for certain users instead of customizing applications for single customers.

Azure Database for MySQL is a fully managed, production-ready relational database service on Microsoft Azure, based on MySQL Community Edition. It offers a flexible server deployment option with high availability, managed maintenance, automatic backups, elastic scaling, and various configuration options.

The service provides multiple compute tiers, storage autogrow, read replicas, and point-in-time restore through its backup and restore capabilities. Its costs span compute, storage, I/O, and replication. Performance can be monitored through Azure Monitor.

Azure Database for MySQL is covered by a service guide with recommendations across all five Azure Well-Architected Framework pillars, including security, backup, reliability design considerations, governance policies, and updated architecture best practices for cost optimization.

nodes.description:
A cost model is a fundamental exercise and decision-making aid that estimates the total cost of ownership for a workload by segmenting and breaking down all associated expenses. These expenses typically include infrastructure, software licenses, personnel, data storage, platform services, user and system flows, operations, maintenance, support, and implementation costs.

A cost model serves as a foundational tool for expense forecasting and budget planning. It predicts combined costs of services and associated expenses, projects future expenses, allocates funds, adjusts for deviations, and evaluates the financial impact of business changes. It is used alongside the budget to review spending with stakeholders, identify cost trends, and uncover optimization areas.

Additionally, a cost model supports budgeting, scenario analysis, and resource optimization, enabling informed decision-making about workload expenses.<SEP>A cost model helps understand, forecast, and optimize costs, and make informed architectural decisions based on COGS effects.<SEP>A cost model represents the marginal cost per customer and identifies how business metrics influence costs in SaaS development.

Service-Level Agreements (SLAs) are formal commitments and business metrics that define agreed-upon performance levels between service providers and consumers, particularly regarding reliability, availability, and expected uptime. In the context of Azure, SLAs represent commitments indicating expected uptime levels and conditions for each service.

SLAs govern workloads and require budget allocation decisions, balancing potential penalties against implementation efforts. They define acceptable levels of system and service operation and are used as criteria to confirm incident resolution. Additionally, SLAs establish predefined limits and error budgets that chaos engineering tests must adhere to.<SEP>Service-level agreements (SLAs) are commitments from Azure indicating expected uptime levels and conditions for each service.<SEP>Service-level agreements (SLAs) are commitments regarding the performance and availability of a service.<SEP>Service-level agreements (SLAs) are explicit commitments made to customers about solution availability, which should reflect composite SLAs of underlying Azure services.

Health Probes encompass several types, including liveness, readiness, and startup probes, which serve distinct purposes: detecting failures, ensuring traffic routes to healthy containers, allowing proper initialization, and enabling self-healing mechanisms.

In the context of Azure services, Health Probes are used by Application Gateway to detect back-end unavailability and ensure traffic only routes to healthy back ends. Azure Service Bus is a fully managed enterprise message broker within the Microsoft Azure platform that enables reliable messaging between distributed applications and services. It provides queue-based asynchronous communication capabilities, supporting queues, topics, subscriptions, and sessions for flexible messaging operations. The service is available in multiple pricing tiers, including Premium and Standard.

Azure Service Bus offers a rich set of features including duplicate detection, dead letter queues, auto-forwarding, partitioned entities, and advanced routing capabilities. It supports ReplyTo and CorrelationId properties for background task communication, as well as message schemas with attached metadata for classification purposes. The service facilitates asynchronous programming patterns such as priority queue processing.

For reliability and resilience, Azure Service Bus supports zone-redundant deployments, geo-disaster recovery, and replication patterns. It provides native programmatic retry capabilities and ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) telemetry. Architectural best practices cover authentication, private endpoints, tier selection, and autoscaling. The service also includes built-in policies for security and governance, supporting high-throughput messaging scenarios.

Azure Service Bus can provide custom metrics for autoscaling in Container Apps and serves various workloads across Azure architectures. In practical usage, it functions as a message-bus technology whose implementation details can be abstracted in block diagrams. For example, in an e-commerce scenario, a spike in failed messages on Azure Service Bus caused payment failures, illustrating the importance of monitoring and resilience. The service also provides guidance on failure modes to help ensure reliable messaging.

Zone-Redundant Deployment is a deployment model in Microsoft Azure that distributes resources, including application and storage tiers, across multiple availability zones within a single region. This approach provides high reliability and resiliency by ensuring that if one availability zone experiences an outage, the workload continues operating in the remaining zones.

Key features of Zone-Redundant Deployment include built-in load balancing, synchronous replication, and automatic failover, all managed by Microsoft. This eliminates the need for customers to manually handle synchronization and failover processes, simplifying operations while maintaining robust availability.

Zone-Redundant Deployment offers high reliability at moderate cost and is recommended for many production workloads. As a single-region strategy, it serves as an effective redundancy approach for organizations seeking resilient infrastructure without the complexity of multi-region architectures.

Data residency refers to restrictions and compliance requirements governing the physical geographic locations where data can be stored and processed. These requirements are often driven by legal and regulatory mandates that dictate data must remain within a specific location or jurisdiction. Data residency is critically important for industries such as healthcare and banking, where strict regulations govern the handling and storage of sensitive information.

From an architectural perspective, data residency is a key concern that varies depending on the deployment approach and region selection. In Microsoft Azure environments, data residency compliance is achieved in both zonal and zone-redundant deployments by ensuring that data is stored within the selected Azure region. This allows organizations to meet their geographic data storage obligations while leveraging cloud infrastructure for resilience and availability.<SEP>Data residency refers to regulations governing where user data is stored, which can affect identity provider choices and require separate deployment stamps for different geographies.<SEP>Data residency refers to requirements about where customer data can be stored, often driven by data sovereignty laws.

Azure NetApp Files is an Azure-native, enterprise-class, fully managed cloud-based service designed for running file workloads in the cloud. It supports NFS, SMB, and dual-protocol volumes, offering file shares, snapshots, cloning, and storage-based replication including cross-zone and cross-region replication for data redundancy. The service delivers high-performance, low-latency storage capable of up to 460,000 IOPS per volume, making it suitable for large-scale deployments.

Azure NetApp Files provides multiple service levels (including the Flexible service level), capacity pools, and performance tiers to support diverse workloads. Key use cases include SAP high-availability configurations, SAPMNT share reliability on both Linux and Windows, FSLogix profiles with snapshot backup support, and serving as an extra datastore for Azure VMware Solution where colocation is critical for disk expansion. It also supports application infrastructure and database workloads.

The service offers comprehensive security features including encryption, access control lists (ACLs), file access logging, network security configurations, and built-in policies for SMB and NFS protocol configurations. Additional capabilities include performance optimization, data tiering, cost optimization, and critical data backup using snapshots with cross-region replication. Guidance is available for security and cost optimization best practices.<SEP>Azure NetApp Files (ANF) provides an Application Volume Group feature that uses proximity placement groups to deploy volumes close to VM/compute clusters.

Platform as a Service (PaaS) is a cloud service model where the provider manages the operating system and shares responsibility for identity, applications, and networking. PaaS is easier to configure and administer compared to Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), removing the need for virtual machine setup and maintenance tasks.

PaaS offerings provide built-in autoscale features and handle load balancing, client-request handling, and state management. PaaS database solutions are more cost-effective and efficient than IaaS by reducing manual scaling, backups, and infrastructure maintenance. In Azure, PaaS solutions typically support zone-redundant deployments.

PaaS is recommended to minimize operational burden for AI workloads and is preferred over self-hosted options to simplify design and automate workflow orchestration.<SEP>PaaS is a fully managed platform that handles scaling, availability, and performance, optimizing hardware efficiency.

Gateway Offloading is a design pattern that offloads request processing to a gateway device before and after forwarding requests to backend nodes. This approach centralizes functionality—such as security features like web application firewalls and TLS connections—reducing the complexity of application code and shifting per-node processing costs to a centralized processing model. By consolidating these responsibilities at the gateway level, organizations can use fewer resources per node and benefit from centralized configuration management of offloaded functionality.

nodes.description:
The Bulkhead Pattern is a design pattern that introduces intentional segmentation between components of a system to isolate failures and contain their blast radius. By partitioning a system into isolated groups or pools, it prevents failures in one component from cascading to other parts, ensuring that only affected sections experience problems while the remaining components continue to function normally.

The pattern can be applied in various ways, including partitioning service instances into pools based on consumer load and availability requirements, or restricting customers to specific regions by treating multiregion deployments as separate stamps. It also serves to isolate services from each other, ensuring independent lifecycles. Overall, the Bulkhead Pattern is a fundamental approach to achieving fault isolation and resilience in system architecture.<SEP>The Bulkhead pattern is a design pattern that isolates failures and prevents cascading failures in systems.

nodes.description:
The Circuit Breaker Pattern is a resilience-oriented design pattern that prevents an application from repeatedly attempting operations likely to fail. It works by monitoring failures against a threshold within a specified time window; once that threshold is exceeded, the circuit "opens," immediately returning errors instead of making further requests to malfunctioning dependencies. This prevents unnecessary resource consumption and avoids cascading failures caused by continual retries to external dependencies.

The pattern enables graceful degradation and is often coupled with automatic recovery mechanisms, allowing the system to self-heal when the underlying dependency becomes available again. By handling failures in a controlled manner, the Circuit Breaker Pattern increases overall system availability, optimizes resource utilization, and enhances architectural resilience. It is closely related to retry and fault-handling strategies, serving as a complementary safety measure for building robust, fault-tolerant systems.<SEP>Circuit breaker pattern is applied to consumer applications to prevent cascading failures.<SEP>A design pattern that stops sending requests to failing consumers after consecutive failures to prevent cascading failures.<SEP>The circuit breaker pattern is used to protect traffic during recovery scenarios and implement client-side throttling protection in Azure Event Hubs.<SEP>The Circuit Breaker pattern avoids continued retries when quotas are exceeded or services are unavailable.<SEP>Circuit breaker pattern is a design pattern that prevents applications from performing operations likely to fail, reducing unnecessary processing.

Horizontal scaling, also known as scaling out, is a scaling approach that adds more instances of a given resource type to distribute workload across multiple servers or compute nodes. A Disaster Recovery Plan (DR plan) is a comprehensive, process-based living document designed to respond to catastrophic failures and other major incidents. It provides detailed, executable procedures for recovering specific systems after major failures, including step-by-step recovery actions, roles, responsibilities, failover sequences, and communication workflows.

The plan covers recovery architecture components, failover mechanisms, user and data flow impact, and operational recommendations to meet Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) goals. It is activated when incidents meet disaster-level thresholds based on severity evaluation, and addresses technical artifacts alongside communication and recovery steps.

A Disaster Recovery Plan evolves from basic graceful degradation strategies at more mature organizational levels. It also serves as a guide for building recovery strategies for multi-region deployments—such as those on Azure—based on business priorities and reliability objectives, covering approaches including backup and restore, active-passive, and active-active strategies.<SEP>A well-documented disaster recovery plan defines recovery steps, RPO, and RTO targets for business continuity.<SEP>A comprehensive disaster recovery plan involves creating a plan and deciding on recovery technology, including handling dependencies and stateful components.

The Workload Team is a cross-functional team comprising members with both technical and business disciplines—including legal, finance, business, and engineering departments—focused on the success of a workload throughout its full lifecycle. It serves as the direct team handling most workload requirements and builds relationships with other teams to co-deliver on workload goals.

The Workload Team is responsible for implementing architectural specifications designed by architects. Its responsibilities span a wide range of operational and technical tasks, including configuring Azure Virtual Desktop deployments, managing user access, monitoring, compliance, and general operational tasks. Additionally, the team handles performance analysis, OS and application updates, key management, and FSLogix management. It is also responsible for application-level backups, data recovery, application configurations, and application-specific credentials.

The Workload Team is accountable for its own documented practices, including documenting any extra steps or intentional deviations from standard procedures.

It is owned and managed by a separate team and serves as a critical dependency for certain workloads.

SQL Managed Instance offers a 99.99% SLA, though this may be adjusted (e.g., to a 99.80% SLO) to account for data operation failures. It supports zone redundancy, failover groups, geo-replication, and managed maintenance windows for high availability and disaster recovery. Deployment configurations include instance pools, stop/start schedules, and failover groups.

The service deploys into dedicated virtual network subnets and provides instance-scoped controls, including SQL Agent, CLR assemblies, linked servers, and Enterprise Edition capabilities. It supports Microsoft Entra authentication, auditing, Transparent Data Encryption (TDE), managed identities, and various other security configurations.

SQL Managed Instance uses an always-provisioned compute model with vCore-based billing and bills for reserved storage. It can be governed through Azure Policy and Azure Advisor recommendations.

Connection Monitor is a feature of Azure Network Watcher that continuously tracks network connectivity and performance across Azure resources. It operates by running continuous synthetic tests, generating synthetic traffic to measure key metrics such as latency and packet loss. The tool provides real-time alerts for connectivity and performance problems and includes diagnostic capabilities to analyze and identify networking issues, pinpointing where along the network path problems occur.

Connection Monitor supports monitoring connectivity between on-premises resources and Azure over ExpressRoute, enabling detection of networking issues across hybrid environments. Vertical scaling, also known as scaling up, is a scaling approach that increases the capacity of existing resources by adding more compute power to a single machine or instance. This typically involves upgrading to a larger server or instance size by increasing resources such as CPU, memory, or other capabilities rather than adding more machines.

Vertical scaling is particularly suitable for stateful applications where distributing workloads across multiple servers may be complex. In cloud environments, it can involve selecting a larger VM SKU or upgrading instance sizes, though this process often requires downtime to implement the changes. In the context of messaging services, vertical scaling may involve Premium tier messaging unit increases that provide dedicated capacity with automatic adjustment capabilities for dynamic workloads.

While vertical scaling can leverage larger and more powerful resources, it is generally considered more complex and less reliable than horizontal scaling. It may also involve higher costs due to the premium pricing of more powerful hardware. Additionally, there are inherent physical limits to how much a single machine can be scaled up, which can constrain long-term growth compared to horizontal alternatives.

Microservices is an architectural design pattern in which applications are structured as small, independent, loosely coupled services, each focusing on specific business functionalities. These services communicate via well-defined standards and can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently.

A key advantage of microservices is their ability to decouple components, achieving containment and isolation in architecture. By segmenting services from one another, microservices reduce the risk of extensive problems arising from single component failures, effectively isolating faults. This pattern is also favored for workload refactoring to gain efficiencies and reduce costs.

However, microservices can introduce complexity, overhead, and dependency issues, and the pattern is not the best option for every application. Careful consideration is needed to determine whether the benefits of isolation and independent scalability outweigh the added architectural complexity.<SEP>Microservices is a design pattern enabling individual components to scale independently to accommodate varying loads.

nodes.description:
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is a security method for managing access to resources by assigning permissions based on users' roles and job responsibilities. It enforces the principle of least privilege, ensuring individuals have only the permissions necessary for their role, and enables organizations to apply access control consistently and revoke it rigorously across systems.

RBAC operates across both management (control) and data planes, covering user and system-to-system communication. On the control plane, it restricts the ability to create, delete, or modify resources to specific identities and groups. It integrates with services such as Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC, which assigns permissions based on predefined roles to promote controlled access. RBAC is applied in contexts including Azure Front Door, Azure Virtual Desktop sessions and infrastructure, Azure NetApp Files, Machine Learning workspaces, network-related roles, telemetry data, and inferencing endpoints. It is also implemented for agents accessing public and private data in agentic AI systems, where separation of duties is enforced.

Custom RBAC roles can provide strict access as a frontline defense. While RBAC offers a structured approach to permissions management, it can result in management overhead related to tracking identities and their associated access scopes.

DDoS Protection refers to distributed denial-of-service protection, a security mechanism designed to detect, filter, and mitigate volumetric and malicious traffic before it reaches application tiers or customer services. It defends against distributed denial-of-service attacks at an abstracted layer, operating at the virtual network or individual public IP level.

Cloud providers, notably Azure, offer DDoS Protection as a native service. Azure DDoS Protection specifically protects entire virtual networks (VNets) and public IP addresses, helping block malicious traffic before it reaches the gateway. Both basic and advanced tiers are typically available from cloud providers.

DDoS Protection is commonly implemented and managed by platform teams to monitor and secure network traffic. It is also a type of service that can be consolidated across workloads, enabling centralized protection for multiple applications and resources.

Conditional Access covers users, groups, and workload identities, enforcing policies based on specified criteria aligned with operational needs and use case restrictions. Application Gateway is an Azure networking service designed for web traffic management and load balancing at the application layer (Layer 7), particularly for HTTP/HTTPS workloads. It supports key capabilities including TLS termination/offloading, autoscaling, health monitoring, routing, and load balancing for web applications. It handles security functions such as TLS termination and traffic inspection at the endpoint level.

Application Gateway integrates with Web Application Firewall (WAF), which can be enabled directly on it, as well as DDoS Protection and Azure Firewall to provide robust security for web applications in hub-and-spoke and Virtual WAN scenarios. It is commonly combined with API Management for improved API performance and is recommended for load balancing HTTP applications with firewall capabilities.

Application Gateway is deployed in a dedicated subnet with Network Security Group (NSG) and WAF controls, and can be used in private virtual networks and multiregion load balancing architectures. From an operational perspective, it can be stopped to save costs, monitored for capacity metrics, and configured with diagnostics, alerts, and autoscaling policies.<SEP>Application Gateway protects internet-facing workloads by creating separation between endpoints.

Azure DDoS Protection operates through protection plans that can be associated with hub virtual networks to provide centralized DDoS protection management. These plans can be created and associated through Azure Firewall Manager, working alongside firewall policies. Azure Virtual Network is a fundamental networking service in Azure that serves as a building block for establishing private networks on the Azure platform. It enables resources to securely communicate with each other, the internet, and on-premises networks, providing centralized IP address management, integrated diagnostics, and capabilities including encryption, segmentation, and connectivity.

Azure Virtual Network offers robust traffic filtering features, allowing users to configure routing and network security groups to control traffic patterns for containment. It provides network isolation and security benefits, enabling applications to securely access resources and route traffic while controlling outbound traffic. It is commonly used to isolate virtual machines and scale sets by defining network security groups to filter traffic.

Azure Virtual Network supports network segmentation and isolation across multiple Azure services. It provides network isolation for App Service apps through virtual network injection, dedicated subnet deployment for SQL Managed Instance, and network-level isolation for Azure Databricks data plane resources. It also enables private communication between Azure resources, supports connecting Azure Virtual Desktop host pools to networks, and is often combined with API Management for enhanced networking scenarios.

Azure Virtual Network provides private IP address blocks for deploying resources with private connectivity, with resilience unaffected by single datacenter failures.

Azure Load Testing is used across a variety of scenarios, including verifying scaling rules and adjusting autoscaling policies, simulating realistic event volumes for testing delivery reliability, simulating realistic producer event rates, consumer patterns, and partition key distribution, and validating capacity under production-style workloads. nodes.description:
Azure Advisor is an Azure cloud service that acts as a personalized cloud consultant, helping users follow best practices to optimize their Azure deployments. It analyzes resource configuration, usage telemetry, workload patterns, resource utilization, scaling configurations, and cost data to deliver personalized, actionable recommendations across multiple areas, including performance, reliability, and cost optimization.

For performance, Azure Advisor automatically generates recommendations based on workload telemetry to help improve Azure applications, and these recommendations can inform performance targets for workloads. For cost optimization, it tracks and analyzes Azure spending, identifying inefficiencies and cost savings opportunities such as idle and underutilized resources, virtual machine usage optimizations, storage cost reductions, server rightsizing suggestions, and savings opportunities for reserved instances and savings plans. Cost optimization recommendations can be filtered for specific services such as Event Hubs and processed automatically via Azure Logic Apps.

Azure Advisor provides recommendations for Azure subscriptions or resource groups and analyzes resources using the core pillars of the Azure Well-Architected Framework, with which it integrates via the Azure Well-Architected Review. It generates recommendations for specific services such as Application Gateway (based on properties like category, impact level, and recommendation type) and is referenced in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL best practices. Additionally, Azure Advisor can detect ExpressRoute circuits deployed for a significant time with a provider status of Not Provisioned.<SEP>Azure Advisor is a tool that identifies VM usage needing optimization for cost savings.

Automatic tuning is a feature in Azure SQL Database that continuously monitors and improves queries automatically.<SEP>Automatic tuning monitors queries, adapts to changing workloads, and applies tuning recommendations automatically using AI and machine learning.<SEP>Automatic tuning is a SQL Database feature that enhances efficiency by automatically optimizing performance.
CI/CD tools are used to automate the deployment process, test against endpoints, check HTTP statuses, and validate data quality.
Self-healing systems automate recovery processes for known performance issues by adjusting system configuration automatically.
Database optimization involves identifying and implementing improvements to handle loads, deliver fast response times, and minimize resource utilization.
Automated monitoring and alerting involves setting up systems to continuously monitor performance metrics and detect deviations or anomalies, triggering alerts when issues are detected.
Automated diagnostics are tools or scripts that analyze performance data and identify root causes of performance issues.
Automated remediation actions are predefined responses triggered when specific performance issues are detected, such as restarting services or clearing caches.

Connection Pooling is a technique that allows the reuse of established database or network connections instead of creating a new connection for every request. By maintaining a pool of ready-to-use connections, it significantly reduces the latency and overhead associated with repeatedly establishing and tearing down connections, enabling high throughput especially under high concurrency.

Connection Pooling is supported by Azure services for efficiently managing database connections, including SQL Database, and is also used as a client optimization technique for Service Bus message handling. Connection pooling isolation can ensure that resource-intensive tasks do not consume all available connections, helping mitigate cascading failures.

However, Connection Pooling can also introduce challenges such as pool fragmentation, which may degrade performance if not managed properly.

Azure Batch is a cloud-based platform service designed for running large, parallel, and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads across tens, hundreds, or thousands of virtual machines. It provides job scheduling and compute-intensive work orchestration on managed VM collections, with automatic scaling capabilities, eliminating the need for users to set up and manage underlying infrastructure.

Azure Batch has consolidated its Low-Priority and Spot VM models into a unified Spot VM infrastructure, simplifying the interruptible compute pricing model and enabling cost optimization for users running batch workloads.

Additionally, Azure Batch has been referenced as a tool used for automating incident response workflows, extending its utility beyond traditional batch computing scenarios.<SEP>Azure service for large-scale batch processing.<SEP>Azure Batch provides automatic retry policies to handle transient node failures in HPC workloads.<SEP>Azure Batch provides managed job scheduling with task dependencies and pool VM size analytics for HPC workloads.<SEP>Azure Batch is a service for scheduling and managing HPC workloads with checkpointing, retries, and analytics capabilities.

Data Partitioning is a strategy for distributing data across multiple partitions or storage units to improve performance, scalability, and availability. It aims to reduce contention, improve throughput, and optimize query performance in distributed systems.

Data Partitioning covers several approaches, including horizontal, vertical, and functional partitioning, each with specific application design considerations. Strategies typically organize data based on commonly used filter columns, with guidelines recommending fewer than 10,000 partitions and at least 1 GB per partition.

While beneficial, Data Partitioning introduces challenges such as synchronization, failover complexity, querying across partitions, rebalancing, and handling uneven data growth.

SaaS, or Software as a Service, is a cloud-based software delivery model and business model in which independent software vendors (ISVs) host, manage, and deliver applications and data on behalf of customers at scale. Solutions serve both business customers and individual consumers, with providers operating the entire software solution rather than requiring customers to manage infrastructure.

A defining characteristic of SaaS is its multitenant architecture, where many customers share a solution while having varying resource needs and high availability expectations. This multi-tenant nature raises important considerations around security, data isolation, access control, tenancy models, and overall design. SaaS solutions often involve many databases, requiring scalable operations, automation, and DevOps practices to maintain performance and reliability.

As a business model, SaaS ties billing, cost management, and architecture directly together, and can be more economical than infrastructure as a service (IaaS). It requires customer lifecycle management and infrastructure management strategies. SaaS solutions can be delivered on platforms such as Azure.

AI is increasingly transforming SaaS, reshaping product design, delivery, and operations. SaaS value propositions can be extended through AI integration across various archetypes and use cases, enabling providers to enhance their offerings and operational efficiency.<SEP>Software as a Service solution operated on behalf of customers, requiring security, compliance, and proper cloud governance.<SEP>Software as a service (SaaS) is a solution model where governance should be prioritized from the start.<SEP>SaaS (Software as a Service) is a business model for delivering software that often involves multitenancy and federated identity.<SEP>Software as a service (SaaS) is a software delivery model where ISVs operate solutions for their customers.<SEP>Software as a service (SaaS) is a software delivery model where applications are hosted and provided to customers over the network.<SEP>Software as a Service (SaaS) is a software delivery model where solutions are hosted and managed in the cloud.
